post_text:
Letterboxing the 61 Johnson St update because nobody watched my three-minute reel about it 😊

.

TENANT COHORT

The site will be for predominantly over-55s and is intended for tenants with low support needs.

The community housing provider, National Affordable Housing Victoria (NAHV), will interview prospective tenants to determine suitability for a lower-support environment and whether they own a vehicle.

PARKING

The project will deliver 57 resident car spaces. This is more than the 48 spaces required under the planning scheme.

While Darebin Council advocated for fewer spaces, we opposed this in response to concerns raised by surrounding residents.

Homes Victoria has advised that the intended over-55s cohort tend to have less vehicles per household (approximately 0.4).

Vehicle ownership will also be considered during tenant interviews.

RETAIL AND FRESH FOOD

Ground-floor retail is included, with the developer to determine its use based on market demand closer to completion of construction.

We have asked for a fresh food grocer to be considered for the retail space at 61 Johnson, or potentially on the vacant land north of Keon Parade, adjacent to the rail corridor.

HOUSING MIX AND MODEL

While we recognise that some people would prefer a mix of larger apartments or a mix of social and private housing, the HAFF funding committed to this project is specifically for social housing.

The proposed one- and two-bedroom apartments reflect demand on the Victorian Housing Register, particularly among the over-55 cohort.

SAFETY AND MANAGEMENT

Apartments have been repositioned to overlook the station plaza and pedestrian walkway, with improved lighting and sightlines to support passive surveillance.

The management office has been relocated to the ground floor.

NAHV will provide business-hours staffing on site, after-hours escalation and a direct contact community channel.

We have also requested a full copy of Hallmarc’s consultation report and will provide further information when it becomes available.

We got there! The Gellibrand Crescent Kindergarten expansion has been locked in, with Darebin Council agreeing to jointly fund the construction of a second kinder room with the Victorian Labor Government.

The expansion will provide 40 additional places, along with upgrades to the existing kinder room.

A huge thank you to Minister for Children Lizzie Blandthorn, Darebin Council, and the Northern Darebin Combined Kindergarten Association for helping make this happen!

Construction won’t start until the next term of government (with the new room expected to open in 2029) but the critical funding commitments have been signed off.

We have also followed up regarding the closure of day care at Merrilands Uniting. There is unlikely to be any change to Uniting’s decision, but if anyone would like further information, please get in touch.

— with Minister Lizzie Blandthorn, Mayor Emily Dimitriadis, Tracey Attard from the Northern Darebin Combined Kindergarten Association, and some fantastic young kinder kids!

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
Doorknocking report for Roseberry Ave, Townhall Ave, and the homes between Gower, Murray, High and Plenty…

— A key issue in Roseberry was the decision by council to discontinue the free neighbourhood street party program. This has affected the Roseberry Ave Christmas party as well as other street parties, with potential fees now of $500-$1,000. We have asked council to reconsider.

— Another issue was the lack of open green space. Unfortunately, council’s ‘Breathing Space’ report treats the astro turf in front of the library as green space (!), which hides the fact that there is a big gap for people looking for a park or playground without having to travel to GH Mott, Wood St or the LXRP playground. One suggestion was to use the old RSL land on Kelvin Grove as a park, or the old police station grounds, or both!

— The plans for Preston Market were a common topic. Key concerns included the scale of development, the need to retain the market’s character, and whether the proposed landscaping and design elements would be delivered.

— We also discussed the controversial protected bike path proposal for Gower St. We need better east-west cycling connections, and there is nowhere else in Preston for an east-west connection to go, but on the other hand, there is also nowhere for the cars to go on that stretch. One possible solution is a 30 kph zone instead of the protected path.

— The complexity of parking arrangements at Sacred Heart Primary came up again. Everyone welcomes the new crossing, but the five-minute parking limit is very short!

— Most people thought the situation with LMCT had improved, albeit with continued frustration about promotional pricing days and vehicles turning right into the station from Gower.

— Other issues included the need for hockey stick marks on Roseberry, whether residential parking permits were being sold to High St traders, the condition of High St shops, the need to plant more trees, the need to preserve local heritage, the need to build more local public housing, rental costs, gas taxation, Airbnbs, and the appropriate speed limit for High St (upon which there are mixed views!).

Scooping a creek for water bugs is a good way to check its health. Finding a diversity of aquatic creatures is an encouraging sign — especially when they include species known to be sensitive to pollution.

Today we joined the Darebin Creek Management Committee for their annual Waterwatch survey at Darebin Parklands. We found caddisfly larvae and other pollution-sensitive creatures — a moment of excitement for us, and a credit to the committee’s efforts to keep the creek healthy!

As mentioned in our previous post, a re-elected Carroll Labor Government will provide the Darebin Creek and Merri Creek management committees with a further $300,000 to help them continue their important work.

— with Kat Theophanous MP and the amazing Darebin Creek Management Committee team, including Peter Grenfell, Kim Davis, Danny Reddan and Annette Salkeld

post_text:
Doorknocking report for the homes between Cheddar Road, Dole Avenue and Elinda Place…

— A number of families have children at Reservoir Views Primary and were pleased about the new crossings on Aberdeen and Greenock (as per photos). The crossings were funded by the Victorian Labor government but delivered by Darebin Council. Some raised concerns about the changes to the Hickford-Borrie intersection. We understand council is taking another look at it. Hopefully the new pedestrian crossings will be sufficiently raised to slow drivers down!

— Other road-related issues included the potholes at the southern end of Cheddar Road (which we have raised with council!), the need for speed humps on Dumbarton, and the general challenges of north-south traffic flow in Reservoir.

— We also discussed the old kindergarten at 2 Dole Avenue, which has not been used since 2014. As is often the case, there is a good write-up of this issue on Serena O’Meley’s website (the write-up is from 2021 on Darebin Independent Observer but not much has changed!).

— Someone raised the very specific issue of older residents from Latrobe Retirement Village and Summerhill Residential Park accessing the Summerhill shopping centre from the Gremel Road side. Apparently, all of the closest entries only have stairs. I guess there is a lift somewhere in the underground car park? Will have to look!

— We also discussed crime, community safety, rubbish dumping, the new social housing project on Johnson Street, vacant homes, Preston Market, the Clifton Hill bottleneck, the responsiveness of Darebin Council to Snap Send Solve, hard rubbish arrangements, and better lighting for the car park near IW Dole (aka the home of Chicken HQ).

We also ran into Rick Arturi of Arturi family fame. Check out Rick & Jessie’s HMS for all your OC, deck restoration, gardening and landscaping needs!

Streets doorknocked: the area enclosed by Cheddar Road, Dole Avenue and Elinda Place, including Daleglen Street, Elizabeth Court, Locher Avenue and Lucille Avenue, plus a little of Dumbarton and Aberdeen.

15. There are lots of steps. How will the elevated levels be accessible for wheelchairs, mobility aids, prams etc?

26. What legal mechanism will guarantee that the privately owned public open spaces (including the elevated open spaces) remain publicly accessible in perpetuity?

27. How much direct sunlight will the existing market receive in winter compared with today?

28. Of the 811 car spaces associated with the market, how many will be available at each stage, and are these spaces shared with the supermarkets and other retail uses?

29. Will there be an in-house car sharing program for residents?

Three-year-old Daisy and her parents, Rebecca and Alistair, are Reservoir locals who are helping make Victorians healthier.

Daisy was born prematurely and spent her first three months in the NICU. While she was there, her family signed up to GenV — a Victorian Government-supported project that brings together data from thousands of children and families to help researchers understand why children have different starts to life.

At a time when medical research is being undermined and defunded in the United States, we welcome any opportunity to show support for our fantastic local medical researchers and the vital work they do!

Happy fifth birthday, GenV! We hope this project continues with strong government support for many years to come.

— with Alistair and Daisy, Rebecca and Matilda, Prof Lisa Hui, Dino Asproloupos from Murdoch Children's Research Institute - MCRI and Naomi Schwarz from Generation Victoria - GenV

post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE – this is a rough summary of where the parties stand at the moment (or any independent candidates aligned with the Save the Preston Market Action Group position). See notes below. Happy to adjust if any corrections.

LABOR – this is the current planning amendment with an assumption of 350 apartments west of the railway and 850 east. See our other posts for more details on the 2023 amendment.

LIBERAL – Liberal MPs agreed with heritage protection but criticised the apartment height restrictions. So this assumes a Liberal/One Nation govt approves the Medich proposal and also potentially increases yield and heights to those in the old VPA plan. An extra 50+ apartments would generate more council rates and stamp duty but the calcs assume the extra revenue just covers the extra services for extra residents.

GREENS – Greens councillors unanimously endorsed the 2023 SAC recommendations (as did all councillors), which included max 14 storeys and 1,200 apartments. As per above, the assumption is 350/850 west/east. Public acquisition is costed roughly at $200 m. It is not clear if they are proposing public housing west of the tracks but assuming only east, that is 850 new units at a total NPV cost of ~$369 million ($16 k annually taken from RoGS annual Vic net recurrent plus depreciation, at a 4% discount rate, plus $34 k per apartment in foregone stamp duty). Presumably the housing would be owned by DFFH and the market by Darebin Council.

SPMAG – their Community Vision Masterplan has two 12-storey buildings west of the tracks, with roughly 360 apartments, and eight buildings to the east with roughly 411 apartments total. It proposes a mix of public/community/private. The calcs assume an equal three-way split. So the assumed cost of 514 public/community apartments is ~$223 m using the same method as above. Public acquisition cost is reduced assuming they sell land worth ~$40 m to private developers for the remaining apartments.

VICTORIAN SOCIALISTS – the same as the SPMAG proposal, as per their position, but with all housing as public housing including buying 30A Cramer (estimated at ~$40 m) for public housing west of the tracks.

post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE – thanks everyone for the feedback on the proposal plans. Below are some follow-up questions we’ve sent the planning department.

— Why are there no official 3D renders or visualisations in the plans?

(The below image is our very rough attempt!)

— Are there any examples of similar elevated green open spaces working successfully in Australia?

— Landscaping elements are often cut from projects when budgets come under pressure. How will we know the elevated green space will happen? If it is not a success in stage 1, will later stages be adjusted?

— Will planning permits be assessed on a stage-by-stage basis over the 2028 to 2035 period?

— Can the 16-storey tower be reduced to 14 storeys and those two storeys transferred elsewhere?

— How does the proposed 10% affordable housing commitment relate to the affordable housing options in the planning scheme? Will 10% of apartments be provided at a 30% discount to a registered housing agency?

— Is the full area of ‘Station Park’ counted towards the open space requirement? Is half of it under a building?

— Can any of the parks be designed as a piazza-style civic space, with cafés etc on the sides?

— The plans say the parks will not be transferred to Darebin Council. What open space levies or developer contributions will be paid?

— The market currently has 864 parking spaces. The plans reduce the parking to ~600 spaces in Stage 1A before increasing to ~1,400 later (albeit shared with new retail and residential). What are the exact final car parking numbers and how will the market operate with reduced parking?

— The first stage of the project consists of a new supermarket on Cramer St (presumably a Coles as per the appendices). Will Aldi return and if so where?

— The planning scheme says Cramer St should be a ‘people street’. But the plans show significant extra traffic. How will this be managed? How will the signalised intersection work given its proximity to the shared-use path crossing?

— We have previously asked if the Murray Rd bus stop could be inset for better traffic flow and safety. Can that be done?

— Darebin Council has been consulted. What is council’s position on the proposed plans?

post_text:
Door-knocking report for the homes between Plenty Road, Albert Street and Tyler Street…

— A key issue was the former public housing estate on McComas and McColl. We are hoping to secure federal support to build new social housing in the area.

— Road safety on Plenty Road was another major topic. We saw a crash at Wilkinson and Plenty when we were doorknocking there in May! There were mixed views on reducing the speed limit to 50 kph but we have been strongly pushing for it.

– Other road safety issues included the need for a pedestrian crossing near Wilkinson, the need for a speed bump on the Albert Street slip lane, the general strangeness of the intersection of McColl and Plenty (including the strange footpaths!), and the lack of safe crossing options on Albert Street.

— Drainage along Tyler Street near Kinkora was a concern for residents in that area. We have raised this issue with council, who have apparently budgeted for drainage design works.

– Other issues included community safety, hard rubbish, food relief, revitalisation of the Oakhill Village shops, parking along that part of Plenty Rd, buses not stopping for passengers around Tyler and Plenty, hot water at Reservoir Leisure Centre (or the lack thereof), housing affordability, diesel costs, the circular economy, federal gas reserves, Palestine, the riding of illegally modified bikes around Darebin Creek and Edwardes Lake, the need to support Australian manufacturing, medicinal cannabis, and real estate reserve prices.

Was also great to door-knock one of our great local activist journalists: Marie McInerney from Croakey - Informed, engaged communities for health!

Streets door-knocked: the area bordered by Tyler, Plenty and Albert streets.

Talking about the oval!

For reasons we don’t fully understand, approximately 20,000 cubic metres of soil was dumped on the William Ruthven ovals between 2013 and 2015 (though there may have already been earlier fill on the site).

Reports describe the soil as “uncontrolled fill”, meaning there is no documented engineering control over how it was placed or compacted. The soil is also predominantly clay. It was not ever likely to create a good sporting surface.

If anyone has any further information, please let us know.

Unfortunately, fixing the problem will require significant and costly earthworks.

-- with Premier Ben Carroll MP at William Ruthven Secondary College

post_text:
Merrilands Uniting Early Learning will cease providing long day care from 2027. Below is a summary of what we know about the issue.

— Approximately 38 families will be affected.

— Uniting says “the centre has been struggling to attract families for the last four to five years” and believes this is linked to “an increase in new childcare centres nearby”.

— However, families have reported that it has been difficult to obtain daycare places.

— Furthermore, it is not clear why a well-regarded, long-standing local centre would lose daycare enrolments to newer centres with typically higher fees.

— The Department of Education and Darebin Council are working to assist families to find alternative long day care.

— Uniting Vic.Tas has been running childcare at the centre since 1985.

— The centre is covered by VECTEA (the Victorian Early Childhood Teachers and Educators Agreement).

We are seeking further information regarding the decision.

We posted this photo yesterday, and then learnt very sadly through his family that Mario, who appears in it with his wife Michelina, had passed away.

We had a great chat to Mario and Michelina back in April. They had arrived in Australia in 1961 and moved into Reservoir in 1967. We discussed a number of local issues, including the Visy plant, and we were grateful to Mario for his considered views and good humour.

Our condolences to Michelina and Mario’s friends and family at their time of loss.

We have reposted the original post below, which set out issues raised while door-knocking homes near the Visy plant.

Door-knocking feedback for the houses around the Visy plant…

— As per our previous post, the main topic of conversation was the Visy odour. There was a wide variety of views, but the most common sentiment was that while the problem had improved, it was not fully solved.

— People also raised noise, dust and odour problems from elsewhere in the industrial precinct, including from Integrated Packaging, Norstar and the ice cream plant.

— School zones were an issue, especially for John Fawkner Secondary College, which is a long trip by public transport.

— Key road safety concerns included the need for a safer crossing on Banbury Road, the need for speed bumps on Radford Road (which council has approved), and the possibility of imposing a truck curfew.

— A couple of people requested more lighting for joggers and walkers at Edwardes Lake.

We also discussed feral cats, land taxes, the abandoned car on Zinnia Street, long-day care availability, the 553 bus, drainage on Banbury Road, Preston Market, Palestine, the Animal Care and Protection Bill, e-scooters, people riding bikes on local footpaths, fishing in Edwardes Lake, the van that was at Edwardes Lake, burnouts in that car park, Gonski funding and rubbish dumping.

Streets door-knocked: the area enclosed by Banbury, Broadhurst, Merri Creek, and Zinnia/Edwardes streets.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
VISY UPDATE – if you are concerned about the odours from the Visy recycling plant, please sign the parliamentary petition via the link in the comments. 

BACKGROUND INFO

Visy has been producing cardboard packaging at the Radford Road site since 1959. The recycling plant opened in 1983.

There is some debate about when the odour issue started. Many people date it to roughly 2020, when Visy began recycling more water and using more household feedstock (which includes more food residue than industrial feedstock).

Bacteria in the plant’s recycled water systems produced sulphides and volatile fatty acids, which can cause strong odours.

Following complaints from residents, the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) issued a series of notices to Visy requiring the company to investigate and rectify the issue. The rectification measures included:

— introducing a bacteria control program (from 2020)
— increasing the use of fresh water for flushing (from 2021)
— switching back to industrial feedstock (from 2022)
— sealing roof vents and building gaps (2022–2025)
— extending exhaust systems and installing new stacks and fans (2021–2026).

Visy claims that the changes have resulted in a 91% reduction in measured odour units at the plant.

However, we don’t believe the reduction experienced in the community has been anywhere near that amount.

We have doorknocked all homes within 500 metres of the plant: once in 2022 and again this year.

While different people have different senses of smell, the odours remain a serious problem for many households. In 2022, we estimated that more than 200 households felt the odours were having a major negative impact on their lives. In 2026, we estimate that more than 100 households continue to be affected that way.

A local resident, Frieda De Doncker, has started a petition asking the EPA to impose further, urgent odour control requirements. We support that ask.

We are sponsoring the petition to provide further evidence about the number of households affected.

We will continue to raise the issue in parliament and with the minister.

post_text:
Hundreds of basketballers play each week at Darebin Community Sports Stadium, both through the Darebin Basketball Association and Reservoir High School.*

Unfortunately, maintenance of the stadium has become an issue.

The stadium has an unusual maintenance arrangement: it is owned by the Department of Education as part of Reservoir High, but Darebin Council maintains the building under a Community Joint Use Agreement.

We appreciate that Darebin Council has allocated $800,000 for staged roof and insulation renewal over the next three years. However, in the long run, it might make more sense for maintenance and ownership to be aligned within one organisation, rather than split across two.

We will raise the issue with the new Minister for Education, Gabrielle Williams MP. We will also raise the possibility of expanding the stadium to the north to accommodate further growth in basketball.

— with Luke Van Rijn and Dain Swetalla from Darebin Basketball Association

*Not just basketball, of course -- as per the comments, the stadium is also used for netball, volleyball, futsal, badminton and other sports.

post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — there has been renewed discussion about development at Preston Market, following the sale of the Tarascio family’s component to their joint venture partners, the Medich family, in August last year.

Any such development would take years to plan — and years to build, across multiple stages.

However, if anyone is interested, there is a large amount of information online about what state government planning provisions would apply. Some of the key requirements are:
— ensure the market buildings with heritage significance are substantially retained, including the large murals, and maintain a working market with a minimum floor area of 12,700 m^2 
— provide approx 1,200 dwellings, including social and affordable housing, with a discretionary maximum of 14 storeys at the northern end and 4 storeys at the southern end 
— include approx 27,500 m^2 of retail floor space, and 5,000 m^2 of office floor space 
— provide a public open space adjacent to the market with a minimum area of 2,700 m^2 and a public open space adjacent to Preston Station of approx 1,000 m^2, with the ownership of both to be transferred to Darebin Council 
— encourage a modal shift to active and public transport 
— ensure adequate car parking for the market and other uses
— encourage loading, servicing and car parking areas to be located underground 
— encourage best-practice environmentally sustainable development outcomes in line with statewide commitments to net zero emissions, and achieve an average 0.5 stars above the prevailing NatHERS requirement for each building 
— provide electric charging points for bicycles and cars 
— provide for the use of alternatives to gas 
— deliver appropriate development staging to allow continuity of market trade throughout the redevelopment of the precinct and to support the viability of business for stall holders.

Note that if any development did proceed, it would probably begin on the two sites west of the train line at St Georges/Murray and St Georges/Cramer. They have maximum heights of 13 and 8 storeys respectively.

post_text:
ERIC STREET UPDATE — the two public housing walk-ups at 15–17 Eric Street have been proposed for demolition.

In the reel, I say that the Minister for Planning has given permission for demolition to proceed. To be completely accurate, a final decision hasn’t been made yet. Homes Victoria has completed the consultation and is preparing a planning application for demolition. If you have any questions or concerns, we can still follow up.

Some other points of note from reading the reports…

— The planning report says the vacant apartments are no longer suitable for housing due to their age, poor condition, fire damage, poor environmental performance and the difficulty of bringing them up to current building standards.

— The heritage report says the statement of significance in the original heritage overlay was not accurate in describing the blocks as “an unusual development of pre-cast concrete walk-up flats”. Nonetheless, it recommends the preparation of an archival-quality photographic record in accordance with Heritage Victoria’s guidelines.

— The preliminary arboricultural report assesses 24 trees within the site itself. It says the concept design may allow some trees in the central courtyard to be retained, including two mature melaleucas. Most trees on the site are exotics.

Patricia ‘Pat’ Sebben and her late husband Stephen made an extraordinary contribution to Keon Park Kindergarten.

Pat joined the management committee in 1978 and worked as an educator from 1985 to 2020, eventually seeing not only her own children but her grandchildren pass through.

Stephen served as the kindergarten’s handyman throughout that period, keeping the 74-year-old hall in great condition.

Sadly, Stephen passed away last month. Minister Lizzie Blandthorn joined the Keon Park Kindergarten team on Tuesday to recognise Pat and Stephen’s contribution, and offer her condolences to Pat and the Sebben family.

Most linear reserves in Preston and Reservoir have water pipes or underground creeks beneath them.

This is often used as a reason why walking paths or vegetation cannot be added, even though other parts of Melbourne have paths and planting over similar infrastructure.

We have asked the Minister for Water about developing a more consistent approach so local reserves can be better used by the community.

Relevant local reserves include:

— Northern Pipe Trail (Melbourne Water pipes),
— Regent Linear Reserve (Melbourne Water and Yarra Valley Water pipes),
— Maroondah Aqueduct Linear Reserve (Melbourne Water pipes),
— Ruthven Linear Reserve (underground creek),
— Elsey Road Linear Reserve (underground creek),
— Union Reserve (underground creek) and

The Herald Sun published an article today that implied that the Northern College of the Arts & Technology (NCAT) might be closed. This is not true.

There is a review taking place of government P–9 and Year 10–12 schools. This review is primarily focused on Melbourne’s west, where some schools are organised as P–9 campuses that feed into designated Year 10–12 campuses.

While NCAT caters for students in Years 10–12, its circumstances are very different. It is a specialist secondary college with programs across the arts, trades and technologies.

We will continue to support NCAT’s distinctive educational model and the case for further recognition of its important specialist role.

Demand for kindergarten places is increasing in north-west Reservoir.

While there are new for-profit centres opening, many families want access to a community-run kinder — and the stand-out option in that respect is Gellibrand Crescent Kindergarten.

Gellibrand Crescent Kindergarten has been serving the Merrilands area since 1976. Many of the staff live locally and have had their own children attend. And while it is effectively at capacity at present, its large site means there is space for a second room.

The Victorian Government has been working closely with Darebin Council to upgrade and expand local kindergartens, including Maryborough Avenue Kindergarten in Kingsbury and Merri Community Child Care and Kindergarten in Thornbury.

We hope Darebin Council can continue to work with us to ensure more children have access to a great community kindergarten close to home, including in areas like north-west Reservoir.

— with Northern Darebin Combined Kindergarten Association operations manager Tracey Attard and Gellibrand Crescent Kindergarten centre director Maria Sorace.

VGSA

We understand an in-principle agreement has been reached for:

— a pay increase of 28.3% for teachers over four years;
— similar pay increases for ES staff, including allowances;
— overnight payments for camps in place of time-in-lieu; and
— a trial of more flexible working arrangements.

The cost is ~$4.6 billion over four years. The offer results in nationally competitive pay and conditions.

An in-principle agreement has apparently also been reached for early childhood professionals with the Early Learning Association Australia and Municipal Association of Victoria. It includes:

— a pay increase of 29.9% over four years for kindergarten teachers; and
— a pay increase of 39.1% for early childhood educators.

The offers incorporate the Fair Work Commission’s gender undervaluation decision regarding the national Children’s Services Award 2010.

The agreements will contain a lot of further detail. They will need to be voted on. In-principle agreements do not necessarily mean an end to industrial action — that will be a matter for the union.

post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — there has been renewed discussion about development at Preston Market, following the sale of the Tarascio family’s component to their joint venture partners, the Medich family, in August last year.

Any such development would take years to plan — and years to build, across multiple stages.

However, if anyone is interested, there is a large amount of information online about what state government planning provisions would apply. Some of the key requirements are:
— ensure the market buildings with heritage significance are substantially retained, including the large murals, and maintain a working market with a minimum floor area of 12,700 m^2 
— provide approx 1,200 dwellings, including social and affordable housing, with a discretionary maximum of 14 storeys at the northern end and 4 storeys at the southern end 
— include approx 27,500 m^2 of retail floor space, and 5,000 m^2 of office floor space 
— provide a public open space adjacent to the market with a minimum area of 2,700 m^2 and a public open space adjacent to Preston Station of approx 1,000 m^2, with the ownership of both to be transferred to Darebin Council 
— encourage a modal shift to active and public transport 
— ensure adequate car parking for the market and other uses
— encourage loading, servicing and car parking areas to be located underground 
— encourage best-practice environmentally sustainable development outcomes in line with statewide commitments to net zero emissions, and achieve an average 0.5 stars above the prevailing NatHERS requirement for each building 
— provide electric charging points for bicycles and cars 
— provide for the use of alternatives to gas 
— deliver appropriate development staging to allow continuity of market trade throughout the redevelopment of the precinct and to support the viability of business for stall holders.

Note that if any development did proceed, it would probably begin on the two sites west of the train line at St Georges/Murray and St Georges/Cramer. They have maximum heights of 13 and 8 storeys respectively.

A second campus for Preston High School! The location of the second campus will be the former Preston Girls’ Technical School site on Cramer Street — one kilometre west of the existing campus.

The announcement has just been made, but some initial Q&As are set out below. If you have other questions, feel free to comment or get in touch.

What has the government announced?

The upcoming 2026/27 state budget will invest $761 million in new and growing schools across Victoria. Preston High will receive a share of that funding to undertake planning, design and early works for a second campus. The second campus will open in 2030.

What are the Cramer Street buildings being used for now?

Until recently, the buildings were part of Melbourne Polytechnic. They have been acquired by the Department of Education. They are not currently in use.

Will the current buildings be demolished?

Those decisions haven’t been made. Today’s announcement includes funding for planning and design.

Will there be a connection to the oval?

Those decisions haven’t been made. However, ensuring good public access between the school, the oval and the playground will be a priority.

Does this change the school zone?

No, probably not. Most school zones, including Preston High’s, are based on the front gate of the main campus. The opening of a second campus does not change the main campus as the key reference point.

INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS UPDATE — the ASU is currently engaging in industrial action as part of its dispute with Darebin Council and other councils over the new multi-employer agreement.

Last Tuesday, ASU members in the rubbish waste teams stopped work for 24 hours.

Members are now implementing the following industrial action:

— a ban on collecting rubbish from a range of streets

— a ban on mowing council areas (except where needed for safety reasons)

— a ban on processing requests received through council’s customer service systems (except where needed for safety)

— a ban on processing and handling library materials

— a ban on processing applications for pet registrations, parking permits, planning permits, building permits and occupancy certificates, and

— periodic bans on litter removal and street cleaning along parts of High Street and Edwardes Street.

For the time being, these actions will continue indefinitely.

— install new street lights and signs at the intersection and resurface sections of Edgars Road and Mahoneys Road.

Construction is expected to finish in late 2026.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
Traditionally, the buyer of a home has been responsible for organising building and pest inspections, not the seller.

This has created three problems.

First, it imposes hundreds of dollars in upfront costs on the buyer, who is often cash-strapped and saving for a deposit.

Second, it causes duplication and waste when multiple prospective buyers organise building and pest inspections for the same property.

And third, it creates risk for some very financially constrained buyers, who skip paying for inspections to save money but end up paying much more to fix defects.

The Allan Labor Government is fixing these problems by changing the law so that the seller, not the buyer, is responsible for building and pest inspections — in the same way that the seller is responsible for a vehicle roadworthy certificate.

This will make buying a home fairer and safer.

Work will start now to develop the scheme, with legislation planned for 2027.

Thanks to Rose and Jordan in Reservoir East for hosting the Premier, Jacinta Allan, and the Minister for Consumer Affairs, Nick Staikos MP, to make this important announcement, and for sharing their experiences with paying for building inspections during their house hunt.

post_text:
Panda Mart has been temporarily closed by Consumer Affairs. See details below.

“Consumer Affairs Victoria has been granted a court injunction to stop warehouse retail store Panda Mart from trading, after inspectors discovered hundreds of illegal items on the shelves of the Preston and Cranbourne stores.

Panda Mart sells toys, homewares, sporting goods and beauty products. The store’s scale, variety of products and low prices can attract large crowds, including families with young children.

In March, Consumer Affairs Victoria Director Nicole Rich issued a public warning to consumers, after thousands of products being sold at the Cranbourne store failed to meet mandatory product safety and information standards.

An inspection of both stores last week identified several items of concern. These included banned candles with flammable contents next to the wick, toys with unsecured button batteries, choking hazards, and flotation devices without adequate warnings.

The injunction effectively closes both stores for 72 hours from 9am Wednesday 10 December, while product safety inspectors conduct a full compliance inspection to identify, seize and remove non-compliant products from the shelves. 

Rich said most items sold at the Preston store during inspections in September this year – after the warning about the Cranbourne store – met Australia’s product safety standards. However, the recent inspections of Panda Mart’s Cranbourne and Preston stores found shelves re-filled with non-compliant items.

post_text:
Today, the Premier formally apologised to First Peoples for the historic and ongoing harms caused by the state and the colony — harms set out in detail in the ‘Yoorrook Truth Be Told’ report.

“To all the First Peoples in the gallery today, and to every community across this State — we say sorry.

For the laws, the policies and the decisions of this Parliament and those that came before it — laws that took land, removed children, broke families, and tried to erase culture — we say sorry.

For the tears shed in the dark, for the silence that shadowed their years, and for the childhood taken, never to return — for the Stolen Generations — we say sorry.

For the violence committed under the banner of the State, and the colony that came before it, and for the neglect that allowed it to continue without consequence — we say sorry.

For the laws that criminalised culture and punished survival — we say sorry.

For the wealth built on lands and waters taken without consent, while First Peoples were locked out of the prosperity it created — we say sorry.

For the silencing of language, and the erasure of words that carried knowledge older than the State itself — we say sorry. The loss of those languages is a loss for us all, for they held truths about this ancient land that we may now never fully understand.

For the forced removal of families to missions and reserves, where culture was controlled, movement restricted and identity denied — we say sorry.

For the policies that stripped First Peoples of the right to move freely, to marry without permission, to work for fair wages, or to live with dignity on their own land — we say sorry…

And to those who carried the truth all their lives but did not live to hear it spoken here — we say sorry. From today, our hope is that your descendants and all Victorians hear these truths and move forward together in the knowledge of your legacies.”

For the full text, see the Premier’s website.

post_text:
Jean is 100! She joined us at Preston Primary to celebrate its 150th anniversary and share some stories from her time at the school in the 1930s…

— She was born ‘Isla Jean Usher’, but Isla wasn’t a very common name back then, so she decided to go by Jean. She was pleased that Isla has now taken off, 90 years later, and that people have finally learnt how to pronounce it properly!

— Both her childhood home at 3 Shakespeare Avenue and her grandparents’ home at 50 Queen Street are still standing.

— She used to get food from the shop across Tyler Street (which is also still standing, albeit just!).

— She got top marks in knitting, needlework and sewing, which were critical skills in a period when mass-produced clothes were less common. At Preston Girls High, she had to hand-sew her own sports uniforms; the school only provided fabric.

I asked if she remembered World War II and she said, “Of course, I was in the army!”. She served with the Australian Women’s Army Service at Camp Pell.

Thank you so much to Jean for sharing her fascinating insights into Preston life in the 1930s and her well-informed critiques of Labor policies in the 2020s 😊

— with Jean Neilson, her son Andrew, Mayor Kristine Olaris OAM, Hannah, and Principal Janet Paterson (who after 19 years’ service is now the longest-serving principal in the school’s history!)

Dr Andrew Kornberg is raising funds to establish a new genetic medicine centre at the Royal Children’s Hospital.

Genetic medicines have the potential to transform the lives of children with genetically based disorders — not quite fully ‘curing’ them, because we don’t yet know how to change the DNA or RNA of every cell in the human body, but dramatically improving their quality of life by changing millions of cells in locations where a defect is causing damage.

This is an issue close to home for us because our daughter, Hannah, has a degenerative genetic condition.
  
The aim of the new centre is to ensure that Hannah and other Victorian children get world-class care as these new therapies emerge.

A big thank you to everyone who supported Dr Kornberg’s recent parliamentary event, including Premier Jacinta Allan, Deputy Premier Ben Carroll and Minister for Health Mary-Anne Thomas.

If you are able to do so, you can donate at flyforthekids.org.au

Earlier this year, we had the opportunity to tour the reservoirs with the Melbourne Water team, and discuss future opportunities to use their landholdings for bike paths and vegetation planning.

Gas usage increases dramatically in winter, especially for older detached houses.

So it was great to visit Sam and Alan on an appropriately chilly morning to see how they’ve electrified their Reservoir West home — cutting their bills and helping reduce our collective reliance on gas.

The Premier, Jacinta Allan, and Minister for Energy, Lily D’Ambrosio, joined us to announce three further measures to support electrification:

— from March 2027, any gas hot water system that reaches end-of-life will need to be replaced with an electric alternative;

— from March 2027, new minimum standards will apply to rentals, including a requirement to replace end-of-life gas systems with electric alternatives; and

— from January 2027, all new commercial-zone buildings will need to be gas-free.

It’s already a planning requirement for all new residential buildings to be gas-free.

If you’re thinking about electrifying your home or improving its energy efficiency, there’s a lot of support available from the Victorian Government, including financial support. Our office can provide details, or check out the ‘Electrify Your Home’ guide on the Sustainability Victoria website.

— with Marcella from Goodbye Gas (who helped with the electrification), Alan, Sam, their little ones, Jacinta Allan and Lily D'Ambrosio MP

post_text:
NORTHLAND UPDATE — as many of you know, a group of white supremacists posed outside Northland with a racist banner on Sunday at 3:30 am.

Photos of the incident circulated on groups like ‘Reservoir 3073’ throughout Sunday and Monday. But many people were surprised that the mainstream media gave the incident very little attention.

We asked people at The Age and ABC why they didn’t cover it, noting that they had covered similar racist incidents at the Shrine of Remembrance, Guru Nanak Lake and the asylum seeker rally.

We were told that there was a reluctance to give a platform to a “pure stunt”. Apparently, the same decision was made last year with respect to a far-right incident with an antisemitic banner.

They also expressed general concerns about spreading hateful views and “giving these people what they want”.

We understand the offenders ran away as soon as they had finished their video recording. Northland security notified police that an incident had occurred, and a full investigation was launched on Sunday morning as the details became clear.

In comments to the Guardian, the Premier condemned the incident as disgusting, hateful and extremist. She reiterated our government’s commitment to inclusion, anti-racism, and our new anti-vilification laws, which target and criminalise exactly this sort of behaviour with penalties of up to three years in jail.

Our office has also spoken to the Minister for Multicultural Affairs’ office about the possibility of having a broader community conversation — including with the media — about the tension between not wanting to amplify images and comments that hurt racialised communities, but also wanting to challenge and reject racism, and ensure people feel safe and supported in their communities, workplaces and homes.

We asked people at The Age and ABC why they didn’t cover it, noting that they had covered similar racist incidents at the Shrine of Remembrance, Guru Nanak Lake and the asylum seeker rally.

We were told that there was a reluctance to give a platform to a “pure stunt”. Apparently, the same decision was made last year with respect to a far-right incident with an antisemitic banner.

They also expressed general concerns about spreading hateful views and “giving these people what they want”.

We understand the offenders ran away as soon as they had finished their video recording. Northland security notified police that an incident had occurred, and a full investigation was launched on Sunday morning as the details became clear.

In comments to the Guardian, the Premier condemned the incident as disgusting, hateful and extremist. She reiterated our government’s commitment to inclusion, anti-racism, and our new anti-vilification laws, which target and criminalise exactly this sort of behaviour with penalties of up to three years in jail.

Our office has also spoken to the Minister for Multicultural Affairs’ office about the possibility of having a broader community conversation — including with the media — about the tension between not wanting to amplify images and comments that hurt racialised communities, but also wanting to challenge and reject racism, and ensure people feel safe and supported in their communities, workplaces and homes.

Parliament report for last week…

The lower house mainly debated the state budget. The opposition set out their response, promising to:

— abolish the Airbnb levy,
— abolish payroll tax for high-fee non-government schools,
— reverse the recent changes to the emergency services and volunteers levy, and
— extend the stamp duty exemption for first home buyers to purchases of up to $1 million (up from the current threshold of $600,000).

As is often the case, they didn’t explain how they would fund those changes. The budget is finely balanced so cutting around $1 billion in annual revenue would either leave the budget in deficit or require an equivalent cut to expenditure.

However, the Liberals didn’t propose any cuts, and appeared to broadly support the expenditure-related measures in the budget, including free public transport for under 18s, additional assistance for family violence victim-survivors, and increased funding for public health services. In fact, several Liberal MPs used their contributions to call for even greater investment in health.

The budget bills will be debated in the upper house next sitting week.

Other highlights from the week included:

— a Welcome to Country for National Reconciliation Week featuring Aunty Annette Xiberras and Nunkeri Tiddas; 

— the upper house passing three bills that strengthened the regulation of retirement villages, builders and pokies venues respectively; and

— a function hosted by Bronwyn Halfpenny MP for members of the Victorian Lebanese community, including Darebin’s own Marlene Kairouz and Nazih Elasmar.

I also caught up with Labor’s new federal Member for Calwell, Basem Abdo. We chatted about a range of matters including what it’s like to wait weeks for a result in your seat :)

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
NORTHLAND UPDATE — Victoria Police have now arrested and charged everyone involved in Sunday’s incident, which affected thousands of shoppers and workers.

The police allege that seven individuals from two rival youth gangs chose the outdoor dining area as the site for a fight. Three of them arrived armed with machetes.

The fighting began around 2:40 pm and spread inside over two minutes. CCTV footage shows bystanders intervening to stop the fights. Fortunately, none of the bystanders were injured, but four of the alleged gang members were.

Security arrived within a minute. Police arrived within six minutes.

By the time police arrived, six of the seven alleged gang members had escaped into other parts of the centre. There was understandable confusion about what had happened, and fears about a Westfield Bondi Junction situation. Retail workers quickly closed their shutters. Many people fled to the exits.

We understand police and centre management discussed evacuation options, noting that people were potentially safer inside stores depending on the risk of further violence.

Stores were evacuated one-by-one and a general evacuation ordered around 3:20 pm.

Two of the individuals involved were arrested at the scene: a 15-year-old from Darebin and a 16-year-old from Melton.

The other five were arrested across Monday and Tuesday. They were aged 18 to 21.

All seven were charged with ‘affray’ (using violence in a terrifying way) and intentionally causing injury. The three individuals who used machetes were charged with weapons offences and denied bail. The other four were granted bail. 

On Monday morning, the Premier announced an interim ban on the sale of machetes, which came into effect on Wednesday.

The existing plans for a full ban on the possession of machetes, with some exemptions, will continue to apply from 1 September.

Police are continuing extra patrols at Northland into next week.

Centre management are conducting a review. 

If anyone has feedback about the way the incident was responded to, we can follow up. 

The Victims of Crime Hotline (1800 819 817) and Beyond Blue (1300 224 636) offer support and referrals for those affected.

post_text:
The events at Northland sound terrifying. We’ve contacted the Minister for Police and Northland management, and will provide an update when possible. A huge thanks to all the police officers, paramedics and other emergency services personnel who have rushed down there. 

UPDATE: the Victims of Crime Hotline offers support and referrals to those who have witnessed crime or been affected by crime. Call 1800 819 817 from 8:00 am tomorrow. Beyond Blue offer counselling 24/7 on 1300 22 4636. 

UPDATE: from jessicajessjay26 in comments: “So proud of the men who tackled and held down one man and the women (my sister included) who tended to the injuries. Shout out to the quick thinking shop workers for calling people into the shops and locking up, keeping everyone safe”.

UPDATE (5:30 pm): Victoria Police spoke to media and provided further information to below. The brawl was a premeditated fight between two groups. One machete has been located. No guns were involved. They also commended retail workers for their actions.

UPDATE (4:00 pm): Victoria Police have issued a statement. We understand there were also other people injured but not requiring hospitalisation. 

“Police have arrested two people following an affray involving around 10 people in Preston this afternoon.

Emergency services were called to the Murray Road shopping centre just after 2.30pm following reports of opposing groups fighting, some armed with knives.

One male was transported to hospital in a serious but stable condition.

Police arrested two males who are currently being interviewed.

The centre was locked down as the incident took place and remains closed while police investigate.

The exact circumstances surrounding the incident are being investigated but it is believed the incident was targeted and parties are believed to be known to each other.

Additionally, investigators are also keen to speak with anyone in the area at the time and who may have witnessed the altercation. 

Anyone who witnessed the incident, has CCTV, dashcam footage or any other information that could assist police is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000or submit a confidential report online at www.crimestoppersvic.com.au.”

Very sad news over the weekend with the passing of longstanding Darebin councillor Gaetano Greco.

Gaetano was passionate about his beliefs, but private about his personal life, and it came as a shock to many to learn that he had passed away from cancer on Saturday morning. Even in his final weeks, he had continued to advocate strongly for the causes he believed in.

He had contested the council elections in October and won 58% of the North West Ward vote — the highest of any candidate in Darebin.

While he left the Labor Party many years ago, he remained well-connected and liked across the labour movement. His name was often raised as the stand-out example, along with Phil Cleary, of a left-of-Labor politician who had unequivocally won the support of working-class voters.

His family has issued a statement on his Facebook page. Our thoughts are with them.

— with Gaetano and Danny at Preston Market

A key theme of the week was electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels. The lower house passed a bill to extend the Victorian Energy Upgrades program, which provides discounts for heat-pump hot water systems, reverse cycle air conditioners and other emissions-reducing home improvements.

In great news, the Minister for Energy, Lily D’Ambrosio MP, announced that ceiling insulation will be included in the program from next year.

We also had the opportunity to chat to a range of stakeholders about the social and environmental impacts of electrification, including Victorian Trades Hall Council, the Victorian Council of Social Service, Environment Victoria and the ETU.

Other key moments of the week included…

— the upper house passing the new anti-vilification laws;

— the lower house passing the first tranche of our building regulation reforms, which strengthen protections against substandard work; and

— the lower house passing new legislation to support e-scooter sharing schemes.

The Victorian Parliament has now adjourned until after the federal election in May.

post_text:
Parliament report for last week…

A key topic was housing affordability, and how governments can help people purchase a home.

If you know someone looking to buy a place (to live in!), they should check out the 'Victorian Homebuyer Fund’ or federal Labor's ‘Help to Buy’ proposal.

Both schemes are similar insofar as they reduce the required deposit (to 5% or less) and reduce the interest rate that low-income earners effectively pay. However, they differ in their eligibility criteria, and the Victorian program is scheduled to be replaced by the federal program in June, so it’s worth comparing them now to see which might suit.
 
If you need any further information, our office is always happy to chase up.

The lower house also debated and passed two other bills: one to increase a range of nurse-to-patient and midwife-to-patient ratios, and one to expand police weapons search powers.

Disappointingly, our expanded anti-vilification protections remain in limbo in the upper house. However, the latest rental reforms did pass! There are a lot of great reforms in there, including longer notice periods for rent increases and a new standardised rental application form, which will stop the practice of real estate agents asking you endless questions about former jobs, former addresses, referees, etc — sometimes before they even let you inspect the house!

— with (clockwise from top) Anthony Cianflone MP, Kathleen Matthews-Ward MP, Minister Vicki Ward MP for Eltham, Minister Anthony Carbines MP and emergency services women celebrating International Women’s Day (see previous post!); Eden Foster MP checking out the new kinder kits; and new Labor MP, John Lister - Labor for Werribee, who gave a very warm, funny and inspiring inaugural speech.

post_text:
Commencing construction of a new kinder at St Padre Pio Catholic Primary!

One of our government’s biggest priorities is expanding kindergarten — building a free, universal program that lets all Victorian children start at age three, increase their hours at age four, and transition to prep as confident young learners.

Of course, building a larger, more universal program requires building more kindergartens. To cater for the increased participation in Reservoir, we’ve built a new kindergarten at Reservoir East Primary School and we’re building another at Reservoir Views Primary.

In Thornhill Park, the new St Padre Pio kinder will also host outside-of-school-hours care for both school children and kinder children, allowing families to do a single drop-off and pick-up. It’s an innovative model that we will watch with interest when it opens in 2026!

— with Steve McGhie MP, Gowtham Rose and Heather Finlayson of MACSEYE (Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools Early Years Education) and Daniel Bermingham, Founding Principal of St. Padre Pio Primary

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
Parliament report for last week…

The key debate concerned the government’s new anti-vilification legislation. For the past 15 years, it has been unlawful in Victoria to vilify someone based on their race or religion. The new legislation expands that protection so it would also be unlawful to vilify someone based on their gender identity, sex, sex characteristics, sexual orientation or disability.

After a long debate, the proposals passed the lower house with Labor voting in favour and the Liberals voting against. The Greens abstained from the vote (and most of the debate), which was unusual. Possibly, they had concerns about the strengthened laws being used against Hash Tayeh and other high-profile Palestinian activists.
  
There is a genuinely difficult debate about where political expression ends and vilification begins. But as part of that, I think we have to recognise that people always have a choice when it comes to expressing a political opinion. They can express it in a crude, provocative way that pits people against each other — which is unfortunately what the mainstream media often prefers, and what social media algorithms incentivise. Or they can express it in more a careful and respectful way that acknowledges the common humanity of everyone involved. In the modern world, the latter is always going to get drowned out by the former. But I still think we have to push people in that direction where we can, and that’s what the new legislation is seeking to do.
  
During the week, I also took the opportunity to raise some local issues, including opportunities for more public art in Reservoir (based on a conversation at a recent Multicultural Arts Victoria roundtable), funding support for schools with a high proportion of DI/NAS students, access to the Regent Linear Reserve, and improvements to local Melbourne Water landholdings generally.

— with visiting Parade College students; and MAV roundtable participants Lauren Mullings, Frances Coppolillo, Michael Tudball and Trent McCarthy

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Updated maps of the Preston Activity Centre were released this morning. Happy to answer any questions but some quick points below…

-- No changes to the heights in the core (orange) -- still the same as Darebin Council's 2023 structure plan.

-- Minor changes to the catchment (blue). In theory, you can already build three or four-storey buildings in most of those streets — that's been part of the Darebin Council planning scheme for a long time. But the actual restraints are the residential over-shadowing rules (which limit how much you can overshadow someone's garden) and over-looking rules (which limit how much you can overlook their windows). The fact that those rules apply in residential zones but not in commercial or mixed-use zones has tended to push any development over two storeys to the latter. There might be some minor changes around that, but nothing that will change the key difference.

-- Furthermore, I understand the six-storey limit in the 'inner catchment' will only apply to blocks over 1,000 square metres, and same for the four-storey limit in the 'outer catchment'. As far as I know, there are no blocks that size in central Preston (except maybe the old Bell Motor Inn and the Parade campus, which they are definitely continuing to use as a school, as per our previous post!). 

Obviously, there is a lot more to the activity centre planning than just building heights -- eg, the parts about infrastructure, green space, parking, notice rights, appeal rights, affordability, etc. But the heights always get a lot of attention (understandably) so wanted to provide some quick information on them.

Any questions, feel free to DM or post below. Can send out more detailed information over email too.

post_text:
Parliament report for last week (the first sitting week of 2025)…

Parliament sat for the first time with the new opposition leader, Brad Battin MP. As many of you know, Battin defeated John Pesutto in a ballot in December, winning the leadership with the support of the Liberal Party's conservative faction.

He began the week with 16 straight contributions on the topic of crime -- many of them very tabloid (such as reading out the details of a murder and asking who in government would take responsibility for it). Unfortunately, it looks like the Victorian Liberal Party under Battin might be returning to their strategy of 2017-18, when they talked non-stop about crime to the exclusion of almost everything else. Fingers crossed they don't also return to that era's strategy of linking crime to specific multicultural communities!

On a more constructive note, the lower house debated and passed two bills: one to improve the regulation of retirement villages, and one to implement our latest rental reforms (including the increased 90-day notice period for rent increases and notices-to-vacate).

I spoke to the Minister for Consumer Affairs, Nick Staikos MP, about the two bills, and also about some similar work we could undertake with respect to longstanding issues at Summerhill Residential Park.

I also took the opportunity during the week to recognise some local contributors to the community, including the Alawi Islamic Social Centre Reservoir and Reservoir High School student Vivien Tang.

post_text:
A reminder that today is the last day to submit to Darebin Council's 'Your Street Your Say' consultation for East Preston and Reservoir East.

The submission page is easy to use, and you can see all the ideas people have already put forward (there's some great ones there!).

Below are some of the ideas we submitted (or upvoted) based on feedback from door-knocking:

-- introduce 40 kph zones generally on narrow local streets with parking on both sides

-- install speed bumps on streets that fit the above description (ie, narrow, parking on both sides) and have high volumes of through traffic (eg Cuthbert, O'Keefe)

-- introduce 40 kph zones for Arundel Ave and Delaware St specifically (same problem as above but also have early childhood centres)

-- plant more canopy trees at every playground (if anyone knows a well-shaded playground in northern Darebin, I would be very interested!)

-- create a 'Keep Clear' at Cuthbert and Cheddar

-- review the issues with the new David/Plenty intersection and Cheddar/Carrol intersection (including with respect to pedestrians)

-- install a pedestrian crossing on Gower St near Preston High

-- install EV chargers at Northland (we've raised this with the owners as well).

Obviously, all these things cost money, and Darebin Council is currently constrained by rising costs, capped rates and the Northcote aquatic centre debt. One thing council does have a lot of is land, including a lot of vacant and underutilised land. People are understandably nervous about selling public land, but if the proceeds go towards new community assets (and speed bumps and pedestrian crossings are important community assets) then it is not very different to selling one block of land to buy another. The size of the public asset base is maintained.

If you want to put an idea forward, search ‘Darebin your street your say’ or see link in comments.

post_text:
Do you have thoughts on the reinstatement of the Tyler Street tram stop?

The old northbound stop was removed in 2016 because the curve of the track meant E-class trams couldn't see vehicles approaching behind them.

There has been discussion about reinstating the stop, either north of the intersection in front of the post office or south of the intersection opposite Tyler's Milkbar (where the old underground toilets are!).

Unfortunately, neither location will support a full level-access stop. There is work underway to bring level-access stops up to Blythe Street, but that's still a long way south.

It's also important to stress that no funding commitment has been made.

However, we're interested in any views on the 'north versus south' question. Feel free to comment or DM!

post_text:
Parliament report for last week (which was the final sitting week of the year)…

The key debates concerned multiculturalism, racism and social cohesion.

The Victorian Government recently named a lake in Narre Warren South ‘Guru Nanak Lake’ after the 16th century spiritual leader and founder of Sikhism. This is part of an effort to more fully represent multicultural communities, First Peoples and women in Victorian place names (we’re hoping to have the two playgrounds under the Preston sky-rail named under the same policy).

Unfortunately, the Liberal-National Coalition spoke against the Guru Nanak decision (and organised a notorious protest against it).

They also voted against a bill implementing two key recommendations of the Yoorrook Justice Commission.

In more positive news, there was support across the parties for the tobacco/vape enforcement bill to pass the upper house, and for the new ‘paramedic practioner’ initiative, which will enable paramedics to deliver more care on the spot without having to transport people to hospital.

There was also strong support for some important community initiatives, including the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, Aus Music tee-shirt day (which raises funds for music workers), Movember (which raises money for men’s health) and the social enterprise Christmas market.

A particular shout-out to Reservoir local Sheila Magoye who has raised $27,000 for Movember since a tragic loss in her family to prostate cancer.

Finally, I took the opportunity during the sitting week to raise a number of issues with the Treasurer, the Minister for the Environment and the Minister for Planning. These included land-banking, craft breweries, Clements Reserve, Edwardes Lake and the Merrilands Estate covenant.

— with Vicki Ward MP for Eltham, Jacinta Allan, Rick Cohen (Worthy Cause), Travis Garone (Movember), Sheila Magoye (impressive Movember fundraiser!) and Lee Tarlamis MP (also an impressive Movember fundraiser).

Colonisation badly degraded our waterways, both through the introduction of invasive species and the displacement of First Nations custodianship.

It’s a credit to the Nangak Tamboree project team that they are seeking to regenerate the Darebin Creek opposite CT Barling Reserve through cultural burns and the planting of indigenous seedlings.

The project is a collaboration between the Narrap team of the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation., Darebin Creek Management Committee, Melbourne Water, La Trobe University and the federal Labor Government.

Thank you to Ged Kearney and Kate Thwaites MP for their vital support.

post_text:
Yesterday, the First People’s Assembly of Victoria and the Victorian Government began Treaty negotiations with a formal ceremony in Darebin Parklands.

As Ngarra Murray, Co-Chair of the First People’s Assembly, said, “Our people have endured dispossession, discrimination and marginalisation for generations. The scars of colonisation run deep. But we are still here. We belong to this Country. Our culture, our languages, our people have survived. We have resisted. It is our resilience that brings us to this powerful moment today”.

“…Treaties are a bridge. Not just between us and the State, but between the past and the future… This is not just a negotiation. It is a step towards justice. This treaty is not just about righting past wrongs. It is about peace and healing. Healing for our people, our families, our communities, our lands and waters, and for all Victorians.”

— with Ngarra Murray, Co-Chair Ruben Berg, and Premier Jacinta Allan

post_text:
Parliament report for last week…

The most significant legislation to pass the lower house was a bill related to tobacco products and vapes.

Under the proposed laws, retailers will need to register with the Victorian Government before they sell tobacco products. A system of fines and inspectors will ensure that they comply with the bans on selling illegal tobacco and vapes, as well as the bans on selling products to people under 18. 
 
The bill was opposed by the Liberals, but passed by Labor with the Greens also voting in support.

The lower house debated and passed three other bills: one that amended tax laws, one that updated consent arrangements for restrictive practices in aged care, and one that repealed obsolete provisions in various acts.

I also took the opportunity during the week to recognise some local community contributions, including:

-- former Newlands Primary principal Ross Dudgeon, who retired this year after 14 years as principal and 42 years in the Department of Education,

-- the team at the Victorian Elderly Chinese Welfare Society, who recently celebrated their 40th anniversary, and

-- the organisers of the Keon Park community day, which attracted over 2,000 attendees and featured some fantastic entertainment, including from Darebin City Brass!

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added 3 new photos.
post_text:
Yesterday, Premier Jacinta Allan visited Reservoir High for a student roundtable on social media.

A big thanks to Charlotte, Rick, Makayla, Indi, Jennifer, Mackenzie, Rosie, Aiden and Leonard for their thoughtful contributions. 

They have firsthand experience of the voluntary restrictions social media companies are now introducing for young people in an attempt to avoid regulation. One of the most interesting parts of the conversation was hearing their insights into which apps seem more genuine about the welfare of younger users (eg YouTube, Facebook) and which seem less so (Snapchat, X).

Overall, the students supported mandatory restrictions on things like:

— creating public accounts
— interacting with strangers and anonymous accounts,
— sharing photos and screenshots,
— viewing R-rated material, and
— scrolling through content for hours on end.

They suggested that these restrictions could apply most strictly to younger users and gradually phase out for older age brackets.

On what was a bleak day for politics in the US, it was great to have such a constructive and considered discussion at Reservoir High School! The students’ feedback will be incorporated into further national discussion about social media age limits.

Door-knocking feedback for the streets south of the Broadway shops…

I doorknocked these streets with Vasilios Tsalkos, Labor's local candidate for the Darebin Council elections. If you haven’t voted yet, vote for Vas! The deadline is Friday.

A couple of people raised Maternal and Child Health services. MCH services are run by council, so Vasilios will follow up on the Darebin-specific matters (including some very positive feedback on support for solo parents of choice). However, the Victorian Government is also running a survey on MCH services at the moment. You can provide feedback there until 1 December (see link in comments).

As you might expect, we had a lot of conversations about council issues, especially Reservoir Leisure Centre. Realistically, a major upgrade of RLC is years away, so we have put together a list of smaller potential upgrades, including:

-- the outdoor areas,
-- the change rooms (including the temperature and pressure of the showers),
-- the keycard readers,
-- the benches in the sauna,
-- the spa reliability,
-- the pool temperature consistency,
-- the toilet cubicle doors in the women’s change rooms,
-- the lockers,
-- the awkward corner of the learn-to-swim pool, and
-- the drainage in the walking areas (so puddles don’t accumulate).

On behalf of a certain four-year-old, I’ve also put in a request for more pool noodles 🙂

Other issues raised included road safety on Delaware St (this is the same problem as Arundel Ave – a narrow street still zoned as 50 kph despite lots of parked cars and a busy early childhood centre!), the Youth Justice bill, the Broadway shopping strip, Preston Market, townhouse development, parking, and the shifting of the police station to Mahoneys Rd. One person told us they had their 21st at the old Edwardes St station -- apparently that used to happen!

Streets door-knocked: Bedford, Bernard, and the parts of Howard and Delaware between High St and Clark/Centre streets.

Parliament report for last week…

As some of you might know, Eden Foster, the Labor MP for Mulgrave, has been away from parliament while undertaking chemotherapy and other treatments for her recently diagnosed cancer.

It was great to join MPs from all parties to welcome her back, and to cheer on Minister Gabby Williams as she shaved her head to help Eden raise funds for cancer research. Together, they raised $27,000 for the Cancer Council Victoria.

The big policy debates of the week concerned the gas transition, pill testing and overdose prevention. The MP for Melton, Steve McGhie MP, spoke about his experiences treating overdoses as a paramedic. Other MPs spoke about their experiences with overdoses and drug harm among friends and family. In the end, the bill to enable pill-testing and other drug-checking services passed the lower house with the support of Labor and the Greens, and against the opposition of the Liberals and Nationals.

Two bills to support the transition away from gas also passed the lower house.

Outside of the legislative debates, I took the opportunity to recognise some people for their contributions to our local community, including Aunty Lynette Briggs, Uncle Alan Brown, Sue Hedges, Tanya Saunders, Margie Davidson, Carolyn Dunn, and Dr Mick Creati from the Victorian Aboriginal Health Service -VAHS, and Marisa Puccio, Tennille Khoury, Lisa, Mary, Hayley, Elisabeth and Honielaine from JS Grey Kindergarten.

The page for Minister Williams’ fundraiser is still open if you have inclination and capacity to make a contribution (see link in comments).

-- with Eden Foster MP and Gabrielle Williams MP

post_text:
This week in parliament, we spoke with the Minister for the Environment, Steve Dimopoulos MP, about why the northern suburbs have such low tree cover and what can be done about it.
 
We also spoke with representatives from Nursery and Garden Industry Victoria, who have a lot of experience growing trees across Melbourne. They noted that while differences in tree cover are partially explained by geography (especially rainfall levels, which increase in the east), they are also a product of historic inequality. Tree-lined streets and shady gardens were highly valued in the early 20th century, but only wealthy suburbs could afford to plant and maintain them. To a large degree, those suburbs remain our leafy suburbs today.
 
But there is no reason why that should be the case. We now have the horticultural knowledge and capacity to make every Melbourne suburb a leafy suburb.

The Victorian Labor Government has begun that work through our ‘Trees for the West’ program, our ‘Living Local’ program, and our ‘Green Links’ program, which funded the current planting by Friends of Edwardes Lake. But there is still a lot more to do. We thank the minister for sharing his thoughts on ways to get more trees and shrubs in the ground.

In other parliamentary news, three bills passed through Victorian Parliament this week: one that improved the regulation of residential parks and funerals; one that reformed the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, and one that limited the state’s liability in relation to the ‘Lawyer X’ case.

I also took the opportunity on Wednesday to recognise a number of people for their contribution to our local community, including Helen Miller, who retired this year after 31 years as principal of Reservoir Primary School! We thank Helen for all that she’s done for staff and students and wish her the very best.

post_text:
Parliament report for last week…

The biggest issue for the last two sitting weeks has been the government's Youth Justice Bill. It's 1,000 pages long and reforms nearly every aspect of the youth justice system.

Most of the public commentary has focused on the minimum age of criminal responsibility, which the bill raises from 10 to 12. But given the evidence on the negative impacts of incarceration in particular (even for relatively short periods), there has been an important, parallel debate about the minimum age at which a young person can be jailed.

The bill introduces a new presumption against detention for any child under 14, unless they have committed a violent crime AND present a further risk to someone's safety. The Liberal Party's position was to change the 'AND' in that test to an 'OR', with the obvious result that more children would meet the criteria. The Greens' stance was the opposite: they sought to prevent the Children's Court imposing any sentence of detention on anyone under the age of 16, regardless of the crime committed or the level of risk to others. For those who followed the debate closely, they did seem to leave a loophole open for higher courts to impose such a sentence. But generally, their position was '16 with no exceptions', which mirrored the position of Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service - VALS and most community legal centres.

The bill includes a lot of other important reforms, including a new system of Aboriginal-controlled youth justice agencies. Ultimately, it passed the upper house (at 1:30 am on Friday!) with the support of Labor, the Greens and the left minor parties.

As well as participating in the debate, I met with the Minister for Youth Justice, Enver Erdogan MP, to pass on feedback from local youth justice organisations.

Lots of other things happened during the week, including important meetings with Gayle Tierney MP, the Minister for Skills and TAFE, to discuss Melbourne Polytechnic's Preston campus, and Lizzie Blandthorn, the Minister for Children, to discuss our recent children's roundtable. But given the length of this report, I might leave it there 😊
