post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE — when we last posted about the market, we were hoping that new five-year leases (then imminent) would provide some certainty to traders and their employees.
 
The idea was that the new leases would run from January 2024 to January 2029. During that period, a revised plan for upgrading the market would be developed in line with the state government’s new heritage protections.
 
However, six months later, neither the leases nor the plans have progressed.
 
Apparently, this is due to a disagreement between the owners.

While Sam Tarascio is the highest profile owner of the market (through his company Salta Properties), his overall stake is less than 50%. The other owners have generally remained very quiet. We have reached out to them in the hope of finding out more.
 
To a degree, no news remains good news. The market is still open. But the uncertainty about its future has definitely ticked up, which is particularly tough for those who rely on it for a living.
 
On a less serious and more positive note, the market features prominently in the new SBS crime series, Swift Street, starring Tanzyn Crawford and Cliff Curtis, and named for Swift Street in Preston. You can check it out on SBS On Demand!

My friend Emma Vulin MP, the MP for Pakenham, recently announced that she has been diagnosed with MND — motor neurone disease.

📸 Juliana Addison MP

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
Parliament report for this week...

— The state budget was handed down on Tuesday. Most of it reflected the government’s on-going priorities, including healthcare, Free Kinder, and the Big Build projects. But there are obviously significant challenges across the national economy with respect to inflation, interest rates and workforce shortages, and the budget reflected them as well. Projected spending tracks downwards from its COVID-era peaks.
 
— Periods of more moderate spending can be tough for non-government organisations, especially if they have lapsing funding agreements. The good news is that all the local programs we know about have been renewed. This includes important programs run by Dardi Munwurro - Strong Spirit, Village 21 and Fitzroy Legal Service (including the Q+Law program). Thank you to Enver Erdogan MP for his support in some of those discussions.

— The funding for the transgender and gender diverse health project at Your Community Health has been made permanent, which is a positive development. There is still some further work to do around the details.

— Statewide, the highlights of the budget included the new $400 ‘School Saving Bonus’, which will help parents with school-related expenses. There was also important additional funding for public hospitals, including the Austin and Northern.

— Outside of the budget debate, I took the chance on Tuesday to raise some issues that had come up while doorknocking in Reservoir. These included road safety on narrow suburban streets that are used as through roads (eg Whitby, Invermay, Cuthbert, Darebin Boulevard) and the abuse of nitrous oxide cannisters.

— Finally, we followed up a constituent question regarding the use of the term ‘geriatric pregnancy’. We can confirm that the Victorian government does not recommend or use that term!

-- The key theme for the week was gender-based violence. The Minister for the Prevention of Family Violence, Vicki Ward MP for Eltham, spoke about the Victorian Government's key initiatives in this area, including the Orange Door Network and Respect Victoria, and the further work needed to eliminate attitudes that drive violence against women. 

-- The lower house debated and passed two bills: one to protect consumers if their energy retailer fails, and one to replace stamp duty with land tax for commercial and industrial properties. Thanks to Angela for chatting to us about her experiences with the reverse vending machine at Edwardes Lake Hotel.

The reverse vending machines are a great way of getting ten cents back for every container you recycle. However, there has been some fine-tuning needed. We appreciated Angela taking the engineers through the snags she encountered while recycling hundreds of drink containers to raise funds for Merri Creek Primary, her granddaughter's school.

Here are some tips we learnt:

-- make sure the container is not crushed
-- insert it with the barcode facing up
-- keep your fingers clear of the barcode
-- only insert the container when the light goes green.

Some tweaks have been made based on the feedback from Angela and others. The machine has been running at 95% uptime over the last few weeks and has processed 400,000+ containers, providing $40,000 back to Reservoir residents and organisations.

-- with James (Visy), Neil (engineer), Angela and Ben (Visy)

Reservoir is a very big suburb, and people sometimes ask, “Is it Melbourne’s biggest?”.

The short answer is “No, but it used to be”. Reservoir is the largest suburb by area within 25 km of the CBD, and as it filled out, it became the largest by population, probably at some point in the 1970s. However, it was overtaken by Craigieburn in 2016. It now sits 6th on the list.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the houses between Leamington, McFadzean, O’Connor and Whitby streets…

— Road safety continues to be a concern, as it was when we door-knocked north of O’Connor St. We’ve included a map with this post showing the location of nearby road safety incidents. Most of them occur on the main roads, as per usual, but nonetheless there is a case for reducing the speed on many local streets and installing speed bumps where there is lots of through traffic. McFadzean and Whitby are probably good examples.
  
— There is a lot of interest in improving the Edwardes St and Spring St shops. We have been talking to council about the laneway behind Spring St in particular (though it seems it will be expensive to upgrade). We’ve also funded Your Community Health to conduct outreach sessions along Edwardes St, connecting people with housing, health and well-being services. 

— We’re following up on a range of renting issues. These include minimum standards for rentals, the amount of information real estate agents ask people to provide, the use of compulsory direct debt arrangements, and the stress of abrupt evictions. With respect to the latter, the Victorian Labor Government has banned no-cause evictions, and we’re extending most notice periods to 90 days to give renters more certainty. We’re also limiting the kind of information landlords and agents can keep on file, and how long they can keep it. And importantly, we’re banning rent increases between successive fixed-term rental agreements, so landlords can’t use that as an opportunity to shop around for a higher bidder. If you are a renter, it’s always worth reviewing your rights on the Consumer Affairs Victoria or Tenants Union websites. There have been a lot of reforms in recent years. People often have more rights than they think!

— Other topics of discussion included local footpaths, support for carers, the route 11 tram, the safety of the Edgars Creek wetlands with respect to lighting, homelessness, cost-of-living pressures and low-flying helicopters.

post_text:
Parliament report for last week… 

-- The biggest debate was about renewable energy. Under our Labor government, renewable energy has increased from 12% of Victoria's electricity generation to 38%. But there is still a lot of work to do to reach our 95% target. And one of the hard parts is building the transmission lines. A lot of residents in Reservoir know what it's like to live next to 220 kV lines. But new wind and solar projects will need even larger 500 kV lines, often stretching for hundreds of kilometres across farms, forests and coastal areas. The lower house debated and passed two bills that deal with the planning processes for those lines and the support measures for people who are affected.

-- We also continued our rental reform agenda. We passed a bill to create our new alternative dispute resolution service, which will take pressure off VCAT. And we announced a new taskforce to crack down on rental offences like false advertising and failing to meet minimum standards.

-- Both houses passed the government's renewable energy targets bill, with minor amendments from the Greens.

-- On Wednesday, I got my flu jab (thanks to Carolyn and the visiting CSL team)! Locally, vaccinations are available through Darebin Council at Preston Town Hall, Reservoir Library and Keon Park Children's Hub. 

-- I also took the chance during Thursday's proceedings to recognise some important contributors to our local community, including Fatima Khatoun, Lina Mostafa, Yusuf Osman, Maryam Sheikh Hussein, Stephen King, Carmen Frawley, Mark Van Rooyen, Nick Konstantinidis and Vahid Kamali.

post_text:
Parliament report for last week…

— The biggest topic of discussion was the extreme weather events of 13 Feb and 22 Feb. We were fortunate in Darebin not to be heavily affected, but other parts of the state experienced fires, power outages and wind damage. A farmer in Mirboo North was tragically killed by flying debris. Most of the debate centred on sensible questions about how best to prepare for and respond to these emergencies. The Member for Monbulk, Daniela De Martino MP, spoke about the loss of telecommunications in particular, and how disconcerting it was for people to find their phones didn’t work — not even for 000 or the VicEmergency app. Unfortunately, the Opposition couldn’t resist linking the power outages to the government’s renewable energy initiatives, despite the fact that the outages were caused by damage to power lines, not generators.

— The lower house debated and passed three bills: one that legislated the Victorian Government’s updated climate action targets (including 95% renewable energy by 2035), one that empowered the government to open new early learning centres, and one that tightened laws around firearms and controlled weapons. 

— The upper house passed the three bills sent from the lower house last week.

— During Thursday’s adjournment debate, I asked the Minister for Public and Active Transport to visit the tram stop at Plenty Rd and Tyler St to discuss future options for public transport connectivity. 

— I also took the chance to recognise the contribution of Dyson Group bus drivers to our area, including locals Peter Dimovski and Gordon Robinson, who have been driving Dyson buses for 35 and 42 years respectively!

— Finally, Queen’s Hall in parliament often serves as an ‘expo’ space for outside groups to showcase their work. Last week, it hosted the Women’s Health Services Network. In our part of the world, we’re lucky to have the Women's Health in the North service and of course the Parliamentary Secretary for Women’s Health, Kat Theophanous MP. It was great to hear about their collective work on gendered health promotion, primary prevention and gender equity.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Parliament report for last week…

-- On Thursday, the Premier moved a motion to formally apologise to Victorians who had experienced historical abuse and neglect as children in institutional care. Prior to 1990, over 90,000 Victorian children were placed into institutional care as so-called 'wards of the state'. The entire parliament came together to acknowledge this shameful chapter in our history and apologise unreservedly.

-- The lower house debated and passed three bills: one that strengthened building insurance standards, one that expanded the scope of Service Victoria to provide online services, and one that fixed a range of issues across 14 acts.

-- The upper house also debated and passed three bills: one that improved biosecurity preparedness, one that revoked certain crown land reservations, and one that addressed a range of issues across justice and transport legislation. 

-- During Wednesday's adjournment debate, I asked the Minister for Community Sport to come out to JC Donath Reserve to discuss our plan to provide female-friendly change rooms at the Keon Park FC pavilion. We hope to resolve some questions about the timing of the work, which will be undertaken in partnership with Darebin Council.

-- The debates in Question Time were boisterous and wide-ranging -- as always! The most noteworthy topic from a local perspective was the Suburban Rail Loop. The government remains committed to the project but the Liberals have 'reserved their right' to cancel it.

-- Finally, Eden Foster MP gave her inaugural speech as the new Labor Member for Mulgrave. We heard about her single-parent childhood in Springvale, her Indian heritage, her career as a clinical psychologist, and how her experiences helped shape her values. It was a great speech -- one to watch!

As parliament resumes this week, I thought I would highlight some of our big policy moments from 2023.

1. Victorians can now study nursing degrees for free (with teaching degrees to follow this year).
2. Public drunkenness has been decriminalised.
3. Sex work has been decriminalised.
4. Pharmacists can now reissue prescriptions for oral contraceptives and UTI medications without requiring a visit to the GP.
5. Private individuals can now buy and use e-scooters through the e-scooter trial.
6. The roll-out of digital drivers' licences has begun. 
7. The phase out of reticulated gas has begun, starting with connections to new builds.
8. New affirmative consent laws have come into force, requiring clear and enthusiastic signals of consent.
9. The double uplift bail laws have been repealed.

It's hard to convey the full breadth and depth of legislative reform over social media, but we're always happy to answer any questions. We look forward to another big year in 2024!

post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the streets north of Broadway shops…
 
— The Reservoir level crossing removal continues to be a big topic of discussion. The feeling is generally very positive, but there are some points of contention.
 
— One critique is that the architecture doesn’t meet the heights of the new Preston station. That’s true, though in fairness, it’s mainly due to timing. The Reservoir upgrade happened three years earlier, because it was a priority. Compared to other stations from that period, it more than holds its own. But since then, stations like Preston and Bell have really pushed the envelope. I remember Daniel Andrews saying about Preston: “If you had told me five years ago people would embrace a design like that, with only a handful of complaints, I wouldn’t have believed you”. We have worked with council to commission some new murals for Reservoir (including a great one by local artist Emily Green) and will see if something similar can be done for the station itself.
 
— There are still concerns about pedestrian safety at the intersections. Notably, there is no crossing in front of Love & Co on the Spring St service lane, where people cross as they head to Reservoir Primary School, the kindergarten or Coles.
 
— Speaking of Coles, there is some frustration with the lack of full-size supermarket options. There are rumours a Woolworths might open on the old library site.
 
— The Reservoir Primary upgrade has been well received.
 
— The state of Reservoir Leisure Centre continues to be a sore point, and something of a lightning rod for the complaint that council’s attention is perpetually elsewhere.
 
— Other discussion points (among many!) included the new Cheddar-Carrol intersection, the lack of a ‘keep clear’ for Cuthbert St, the one-hour parking limit on Broadway, the possibility of removing some of the central parking on Broadway, and the need for additional street trees. Given the sweltering heat, we would have definitely supported more!

Thanks to the team at Northside broadway for some much-needed rehydration.

The Reservoir Suburban Revitalisation Board is currently looking for projects that will enhance the area so if you have any ideas not captured above, let us know.

Streets door-knocked: those between Broadway and Carrol, including parts of Cheddar, Cuthbert, Orrong, Royal Parade, Marchant, Whitelaw and Lane Cres.

post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the streets west of Reservoir Primary…

-- We had some great discussions about making better use of the linear reserve that runs from Ruthven Station to Edgars Creek. The reserve used to be a small creek itself, but was concreted over when the area was subdivided. One option would be to build a bike path along it, linking the Northern Pipe Trail with Edwardes Lake Park. Council has flagged that possibility in its strategic documents.

-- The state government’s major upgrade of Reservoir Primary has been very well received.

-- There was significant concern about crime and community safety. We have passed on some specific matters to police. A lot of people think the relocation of the police station to Mahoneys Rd reduced safety in the area. I'm not sure police would agree -- the new station is bigger and better, with a dedicated family violence unit, and patrols in the area continue at the same rate. But there is work underway separately to provide more outreach and social inclusion services around Edwardes St.

-- There was also concern about speeding and road safety. There was some disgruntlement with the fact that outside of school areas, Darebin Council appears to have installed most of its 40 kph zones south of Separation Street.

-- Other topics of discussion included electricity outages, housing affordability, Preston Market, stray cats, street lighting, the laneway behind KFC, uneven footpaths, the lack of signage for the new speed limit on Cheddar Road, the negative consequences of townhouse development, the geographic distribution of council spending in general, and the strong local commitment to Christmas decorations (there is a place on Broadhurst with a great cast of inflatable characters, all lit up with fairy lights)!

Streets door-knocked: those enclosed by McFadzean Ave, O'Connor St, Whitby St and Broadhurst Ave.

Instead of offering the usual ten-year leases to community early childhood centres, Darebin is only offering two years while it conducts a review of rents, fees and charges.

Many of these centres have been around for decades. They have earned the right to security of tenure. 

Please sign the petition calling on council to reconsider its position and give centres longer leases without increased charges. See the link in the comments below.

PRESTON MARKET UPDATE -- it has continued to be a difficult time for traders and workers. However, we understand the majority owners are likely to extend the existing lease arrangements until 2028 while they work through the Victorian Government's new planning controls. If this does happen, it will be a positive development and provide some medium-term certainty.

Obviously, traders will need to see the terms and conditions, and will make their own decisions about negotiations.
 
Some further updates and details...

-- If the owners do extend the lease arrangements and start the development of a new plan, it will probably take several years.
 
-- There is no requirement for further community consultation as part of the development of a new plan. The community feedback from the previous process has been incorporated into the planning scheme. However, we expect the owners will carry out further engagement.
 
-- There have been questions about the meaning of 'substantially retain the existing footprint' in the previous update. Ultimately, it is a matter for the minister, but our expectation is that it would mean retaining the core structures around the Centreway and Strand, which constitute roughly two-thirds of the market. There would be flexibility to relocate parts of the market if doing so supported maintenance upgrades or trading continuity.
 
-- There have been questions about the impact of the new Housing Statement. It designates central Preston as an activity centre. However, this is not a major change. It was already an activity centre under previous strategic documents and there will be no changes to the planning controls that apply to the market.
 
-- VCAT is currently hearing a dispute regarding the permits to build a 14-storey apartment building on the Murray Road side of the site.
 
-- There has been a rumour circulating that Aldi and Centrelink are being evicted. However, they both have long-term leases and it doesn't appear to be true.
 
-- Finally, as many people know, Sunrise will be broadcasting from the market next week! We're not sure of the exact date but will keep an eye out!

Over the last two weeks, I’ve received hundreds of emails and messages about the events in Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. 

We have all been horrified by the suffering and loss.

Many government MPs spoke about the issue in parliament this week. Our contributions reflected our different perspectives, but we were united in our belief that the priority for the Victorian Government must be our own multicultural communities.

Thousands of Palestinian and Jewish Victorians have friends or family caught up in the conflict. Many are fearful and anxious. Social media content can compound their anxiety. One-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Palestinian suffering circulate in our Muslim communities, and one-sided posts that fail to acknowledge Israeli suffering circulate in our Jewish communities.

The priority for the Victorian Labor Government, as the Premier has made clear, is to provide love and support to all Victorians who have friends or family in Israel, Gaza or the West Bank, regardless of their religion or race. The last two weeks have been incredibly tragic for some, and traumatic for most. People who have spent their lives hoping for peace have seen it ripped away again.

We have spoken with affected local residents. Our thoughts are with them. We will provide any support we can during this time of worry, suffering and grief.

Door-knocking feedback for the houses south of DR Atkinson Reserve...
 
-- It was great to get out door-knocking again ahead of the Voice referendum. A lot of people had already voted, or already made up their minds, but some people were still thinking about it. We chatted to them about Victoria's First Peoples Assembly and how the Voice will make a practical, positive difference.
 
-- Townhouse development was a common concern, as it is in many parts of the electorate. If you're interested, there is a good SGS report online showing how population growth in our area has been strongly driven by townhouses, many of which are a long way from public transport options. Darebin Council is assessing the cumulative impact of these decisions on roads, parking and services as part of its housing strategy.
 
-- Community safety and crime were also issues. A reminder that the best thing any of us can do to help combat crime is to report incidents to Crime Stoppers or Reservoir police. Even if it doesn't seem like police can do anything about an incident, reporting it means they can see patterns and respond to them. If there is a spike in a particular location, they will put resources into it. A couple of people mentioned the story of the Banff Street milk bar worker who chased away two armed robbers with a baseball bat. Probably fair to say that is not the recommended way to help combat crime!
 
-- As we all know, there is a perception that council spends more in the south than the north. That came up occasionally.
 
-- Finally, we were lucky enough to door-knock Adele McBride (pictured), who has worked in the office of the Cooper/Batman federal MP for thirty years (and she’s still going strong with Ged Kearney)! Adele has done an amazing amount of work for the Darebin community and we are very grateful to her for it.
 
Streets door-knocked: parts of Banff St, Dundee St and Darebin Blvd between Greenock and Invermay. We got rained out a bit, so if we missed you, we will come back!

-- creating better east-west bike paths by using the Melbourne Water linear reserves and fixing up the Darebin/Merri ends of the Gower/Cramer path

-- creating a path along Edgars Creek

-- bringing the Darebin Creek Trail closer to the creek between East Preston Substation and East Preston Islamic College (and bringing it over to the western side of the creek)

-- adding more 'shared use path' crossings for existing paths 

-- improving the national standards for shared-use-path crossings so they're more visible to motorists (at the moment there is no flashing light option for them)

-- introducing 30 kph zones for areas with lots of pedestrians and cyclists

-- fixing some of the kinks in the Northern Pipeline Trail

-- connecting the Northern Pipeline Trail to Keon Park station

-- planting more trees and vegetation along the Northern Pipeline Trail

-- finding a long-term fix for the Boldrewood and Broadway roundabout so people can safely cycle through it (which realistically would probably mean closing one of the exits), and

-- putting a fence inside the Preston Cycling Club velodrome so it doubles as a dog park (not really a cycling policy but an interesting idea!).

post_text:
DISCOVER LOCAL -- La Goût Afrique has to be the coolest and most improbable restaurant in Melbourne right now (attention Broadsheet Melbourne!): a West African eatery set in a 1970s-era Reservoir milk bar, offering egusi soup, attieke and jollof rice alongside Wizz Fizz, cigarettes and copies of Il Globo.
 
Owner and chef Evette Quoibia came to Australia as a refugee and started La Goût Afrique with the same entrepreneurial spirit as many Melbourne migrants. She knew people would enjoy her cooking, which brings together Liberian, Ivorian and Ghanian elements (the three countries through which her family moved as they fled war). She could see a gap in the market for West African cuisine. And establishing the restaurant in the Moira Ave milk bar helped her support her family.
 
You can read more about Evette's story in the July issue of The Rezzadent. But if you haven't already, get along to La Goût Afrique and check out her cooking!

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
PRESTON MARKET Q&As -- below are some questions that came up during Saturday’s rally. I thought I would post them for anyone interested.

[UPDATE: for clarity, note that the letter in the photo is from the majority owners to the traders (not from me!). See details below.]
 
Does the new planning scheme protect the market entirely?
 
Not entirely. It requires any redevelopment to substantially retain the existing market buildings, substantially retain the existing location, and fully retain the existing size (12,700 square metres). That means all the existing sections would have to stay. But there is some flexibility to move them around within the current footprint, and some flexibility to close parts of the market and rebuild them elsewhere, if doing so was necessary to achieve the overall objectives of the planning scheme.
 
What about the problems with the sewers and other infrastructure?
 
The planning scheme allows for necessary maintenance work to happen. How that work is funded is a separate question.
 
Why is there a ten-storey height limit across the market? Does that mean a developer can put a ten-storey building on it?
 
No. The heritage guidelines prevent any construction on top of the heritage-protected structures. If part of the market were demolished and moved elsewhere, the ten-storey limit would apply to any new buildings in that space.  
 
Are the discretionary heights higher than expected?
 
Yes and no. They're the heights from the Standing Advisory Committee report. In the end, there was universal support for the report across council and community groups.
 
What about the effect of disruption on traders?
 
Under the new planning scheme, any redevelopment proposal would need to include a market continuity plan, which would demonstrate how trading and shopper access would be maintained during construction.
 
What about the threat to close in January 2024?
 
Attached to this post is a photo of the latest letter from the majority owners (from 31 July). It defers any potential closure until May 2024.
 
What happens now? 
 
From a Victorian Government perspective, the planning scheme is complete. All the documents are online and the scheme is in force. 

The majority owners have indicated that they will consider their options and provide further guidance.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP Shared from Instagram
post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE -- the new planning scheme has been released! The key details are as follows.

-- The market must be substantially retained in terms of its location, form and character. This means the idea of demolishing most of the market and moving it to the south-east corner is off the table.
  
-- The core features of the market -- the Centreway, the fruit and vegetable shed, the meat and seafood section, and the deli -- now have strong heritage protection. This was the priority for thousands of people we've spoken with over the last twelve months and it's great that Minister Sonya Kilkenny MP has listened and acted upon it.

-- The new scheme allows for substantial apartment development on the site, ranging from 14 storeys on Murray Road (which council had already approved) to four storeys on Cramer Street. In all likelihood, these new buildings would go up incrementally over a decade or more. The existing carparks would be shifted underground. At this stage, it's hard to say what the final form would look like.

-- While the scheme appears to allow ten-storey heights over the existing market, I think the heritage overlay would prevent that. I'm not sure if in theory we could end up with a Melbourne Central shot-tower scenario (for those old enough to remember that!). 
  
-- The release of the scheme does *not* mean development can commence. There are two further approval steps: (1) the 'development plan', which shows how the overall requirements of the site would be met; and (2) the individual planning permits. The Minister continues to be the responsible authority for those decisions. She has considerable discretion over how she handles them.
  
We will provide a further update once we've had a chance to chat with the owners, the traders, the council and community members. Any questions, let us know.

[UPDATE: I removed the initial comment about car parking spaces because I don't think it was correct. We are confirming, but there doesn't seem to be a minimum requirement in the overlay.]

post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE -- thanks to the Treasurer, Tim Pallas, for joining us at Rustic Bean to discuss the market.

The Minister for Planning, Sonya Kilkenny MP, also met recently with the Save the Preston Market group and a representative group of traders.

Some of the key points of discussion were:

-- the uncertainty facing the traders and workers,

-- the potential heights of any new buildings (the Standing Advisory Committee report is unclear about this, but we've pushed for a single-storey limit on the Centreway and its adjacent buildings, seven storeys elsewhere, and fourteen storeys only in the north-west corner where council has already given approval), 

-- the possibility of shifting some of the residential development away from the market and towards the government land near the station, and

-- the potential trade-offs between keeping the market exactly as it is and fixing its underlying infrastructure problems.

The latter conversation has been going on for a long time, and it has been hard to get clear details, but there are certainly a number of traders who are worried about the choice between continuing to trade in an environment with potential health and safety concerns, having to close their business while an upgrade takes place, or having to relocate their business (possibly multiple times) in order to continue trading. 

We are expecting the Minister for Planning to release the planning amendment shortly. It won't solve every problem, but hopefully it will at least reset the debate towards a more positive discussion about how the market can be retained.

post_text:
INTERVIEW WITH ANN MCGREGOR -- Ann was recently awarded an OAM for her 47 years of volunteer work with Merri Creek. She kindly agreed to answer a few questions for us.

Q: What was it that led you to found the Brunswick Merri Creek Action Group back in 1976?

Soon after my husband Bruce and I moved into Brunswick in 1976, we went on a walk along the Merri, organised by Brunswick Community Group. We almost needed a machete to hack through the head-high weeds, but the valley along the gurgling creek had potential as parkland in a suburb that had few parks. A looming threat was a freeway reservation right along the creek valley. A few of us founded the Brunswick Merri Creek Action Group, and we started learning about the challenges and opportunities in waterway restoration.

Q: What's the greatest change that you've seen in the creek over that period?

The greatest change has been the revegetation: replacement of weeds with indigenous trees, shrubs and groundcovers. That has brought people back to the valley, and many native birds and other wildlife.

Q: What is your number-one priority for Merri Creek today?

Protecting the Creek valley from inappropriate development, and expanding its restored bushland corridor for wildlife and people.

Q: What would you say to a young person interested in environmental activism?

The environment desperately needs our help, and joining an environmental volunteer group is a great way to meet like-minded people and gain a whole variety of knowledge and skills. It could even help you towards an environmental career. Seeing results on-the-ground, or other changes that you have been working for, is very satisfying!

[If you are interested in joining Friends of Merri Creek, check out their website or other friends groups like Friends of Edwardes Lake or Friends of Darebin Creek]

post_text:
PRESTON MARKET UPDATE -- there has been some significant media coverage of Preston Market over the last two weeks, so I thought I would post an update and recap.

-- On 3 April, the Minister for Planning announced that she would release an amendment to protect the market, based on the report of the Standing Advisory Committee and feedback from the community. She indicated that the amendment would take a couple of months to complete. 

-- That's what's happening at the moment. As most people know, the market is already protected by Darebin Council's nine-metre height limit, but the state government amendment will be more comprehensive, with a heritage overlay and other protections. The minister has made some public comments regarding her intentions but nobody will know the precise details until her department finishes its work and the minister signs it off.

-- As per our previous posts, I've asked the minister's team to look particularly closely at height restrictions and land use terms that would effectively guarantee that the Centreway and its adjacent buildings could only be used as a single-storey market. 

-- The lead owner of the market, Salta Properties, has continued to make the same line of argument they have made for the last twelve months. They say the market loses money in its current form and would continue to lose money under any of the proposed upgrades. It can only survive through some sort of subsidy. Their proposal is to subsidise an upgrade of the market from the profits of the proposed residential and retail redevelopment. If the government lets them build enough new retail spaces and apartments, they will upgrade the market. If not, they will have to close it -- or at least, the parts they own. As of last week, they have nominated January 2024 as a potential closure date.

-- Obviously a closure of some or all of the market would be a terrible outcome in general, but it would be particularly difficult for hundreds of affected traders and employees. Many of them would lose their incomes. Some would lose a substantial portion of their life savings. We are looking at how the government could support people in that scenario, if it eventuated.

-- Having said that, it's important to stress that the idea of cross-subsidising the market's upgrade to save it from closure is not something the minister will be taking into account as she works through her final decision. The Standing Advisory Committee report provides a summary of the factors the minister will consider. It does include some cross-subsidy proposals (for example, the proposal from Darebin Council that some of the profits from the redevelopment be used to fund a new multipurpose centre for council). But there is no mention of cross-subsidising the upgrade of the market. 

-- I have said to both the planning teams and Salta that it is frustrating that the public process hasn't engaged with the issue of the market's financial viability. There are some things we would all like to know in that regard. However, my impression from those discussions is that rather than analysing the various hypotheticals, people are waiting for the amendment to come out first.

-- The amendment will be finalised in the next few weeks. We'll know more after that.

-- In the meantime, there are links below to the Standing Advisory Committee report and the 12 May shire hall meeting organised by the Save the Preston Market Action Group, which covered these issues in detail. As always, if you have any questions, you can email, call or DM.

More trains, more often! 🚂 From Monday, there will be another 35 services per week on the Mernda line. The new timetable includes:

•  three more city-bound morning peak services,
•  two more Mernda-bound afternoon peak services,
•  more express services during peak periods (travelling non-stop between Victoria Park and Jolimont), and

post_text:
Today, as part of the state budget, the Andrews Labor Government announced the end of native timber harvesting from 1 January 2024.

This will be welcome news for groups like Newlands Friends of the Forest, who have campaigned for the original 2030 end date to be brought forward.

But as I'm sure they would agree, it will be a difficult day for Victoria's native timber workers, who will need to retrain or relocate on a shorter timeline. It will be a difficult day for their families, businesses and communities. And it won't magically save our forest-based threatened species. Climate change and introduced species will continue to be very significant threats to their futures.

But to the degree that protecting biodiversity is about comprehensive reserves, the ending of native timber harvesting in Victoria remains a historic decision, and one that is almost unprecedented in its scale. There will be a lot of work to do to implement the conservation arrangements and the worker transition programs. As a Labor government, we are very committed to both those components. If you have any questions, let us know.

post_text:
Last week in parliament, I talked about the Boldrewood and Broadway roundabout, and in particular the speed that some vehicles travel through it. Legally speaking, it is a 60 kph zone, and while most drivers slow down on their approach, a significant proportion accelerate once they're in the roundabout -- even when school children are trying to cross at the exits.

To make the roundabout safer, we are working with Darebin City Council to extend the 40 kph school zone outside Reservoir East Primary School so it covers the entire roundabout, including the pedestrian crossings and the Broadway, Strathmerton, Boldrewood and Gisborne approaches.

We are also making changes to the signs, pavement markings and road markings.

The impact of those changes will be monitored. In the long run, more significant works might be needed. The roundabout was built in the 1950s and there are aspects of its design that wouldn't be replicated today, especially given its closeness to the school and other community infrastructure, and its proposed role in Darebin's strategic cycling strategy.

-- with Mayor Julie Williams for Darebin

post_text:
KEON PARK PROJECT UPDATE -- below are some answers to questions we've been asked recently.

-- People have asked about access to the new station from Johnson Street. The good news is that after feedback from our door-knocking, the project team have updated their plans so that pedestrians and cyclists will be able to access the station from a dedicated crossing in front of the milk bar (between Arundel and Liston).
-- Under the current proposal, cars will be able to exit the carpark into Johnson Street, but not enter. They will be able to exit and enter from High Street, but they won't be able to enter by making a right-hand turn. This will address concerns about the carpark being used as a shortcut.
-- The land on the eastern side of the main site, along Johnson Street, is publicly owned. A portion of it will be used for pedestrian and bike access, as per above. A portion will be used for green space. The remaining block (opposite Bambams) might be used for future apartments.
-- With the support of Darebin City Council, Keon Park Boxing Gym has been relocated to Reservoir Leisure Centre (thanks Mayor Julie Williams for Darebin and team for your help!). The old club rooms will be demolished in the next month or so.
-- The design of the station will be by the same architects who did Preston Station.
-- Some people have suggested installing pedestrian bridges or underpasses at Hughes Parade or Keon Parade. We've gone through these suggestions with the project team. The short story is that pedestrians often ignore bridges or underpasses if they think they can cross at ground level. That's why bridges and underpasses generally accompany freeways or train lines where crossing at ground level is impossible. For Keon Parade and Hughes Parade, people are going to want to cross at ground level, and traffic lights are the safest way to allow that.
-- There won't be toilets at the new station.
-- People have asked about a bike path connection along the railway to Reservoir station and the Northern Pipe Trail. The challenge here is the section near Ruthven where there is no path. Fixing that issue is not within the scope of the Keon Park project, but we're looking into it separately.

If you have any further queries, let us know!

post_text:
New pedestrian and bike crossings have been installed at Cramer Street and Oakover Road as part of the level-crossing removal project.

There is always extra risk when road conditions change, and anyone driving along Cramer Street or Oakover Road should take extra care approaching the crossings. We've already heard about some near misses and at least one collision with a cyclist.

On behalf of locals, Kat Theophanous MP and I have raised a number of safety concerns with the level crossings project team and asked that they assess these areas and install additional signage.

Technically, the Cramer Street and Oakover Road crossings are 'shared use path' crossings, which differ from zebra crossings. Cyclists are not required to dismount, and while cyclists are advised to slow down, motorists must ensure they can safely give way to a cyclist travelling at any speed. 

The crossings are marked with yellow paint and give-way signs, in accordance with the standard design. At Cramer Street and Oakover Road, they are also raised for extra safety (these raised crossings are known in Australia as 'wombat crossings', for reasons nobody really understands!).

If you have any thoughts or feedback on the new crossings, or any other aspects of our cycling infrastructure, please let us know. We are very committed to supporting our cyclists and making sure that as many people as possible can ride conveniently and safely.

Free kinder is a really important initiative. Back in 1872, the Victorian government began offering free, universal education for primary school students. We're now doing the same thing for the earlier years.

Starting this year, kinder will be entirely free for sessional kindergartens that offer 15 hours per week for four-year olds or 5 to 15 hours per week for three-year olds.

If your child attends one of these programs within a long day care setting, a $2,000 subsidy will offset the kindergarten component of your fees.

Over the next decade, the government's support will expand, so that by 2032, every Victorian four-year old will have access to a free, universal 30-hour program.
 
See the comments for more information.

The new parliament sat for the first time this week, and I wanted to share some figures on gender equality within the Labor government.

• For the first time in Victoria's history, more than half of the government MPs are women (54%).
• For the first time in history, more than half of the ministers are women -- 14 out of 22 (64%).
• Overall, the parliament consists of 128 MPs, of whom 62 are women (48%). 

In 2015, the Labor Party committed to a gender equality target of 50% by 2025. It's exciting to be part of the first Victorian parliament to achieve that goal! You can read more about our whole-of-government commitment to diversity here:

https://www.vic.gov.au/dpc-diversity-and-inclusion-strategy-2019-2021

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the houses near Newlands Primary School…

-- There was a lot of positive support for Labor's plan to bring back the State Electricity Commission (SEC).
-- A number of people raised the pandemic health measures, from a variety of perspectives.
-- Parking was a concern on Union Street.
-- Turning right into Regent was a concern on Sheffield Street.
-- Given the recent heavy rain, we discussed storm water drainage issues, including on Sheffield Street and the northern end of George Street.
-- We also discussed a lot of other issues: the NDIS, urban forests, climate change, the Victorian Labor Government's medically supervised injecting rooms, Preston Market, Jack Mundey, over-development, bail reform, and Labor's proposed upgrade to the Northern Hospital emergency department.

That's it for our door-knocking reports before the election! If I'm lucky enough to be elected, they will be a starting point for what we do. If someone else is elected, I hope they will be useful for them too. 

Hugely grateful to everyone who answered their door and had a chat, and to our fantastic volunteers -- couldn't have done any of it without them.

Streets door-knocked: those enclosed by Furner Street, Union Street, Regent Street, Clara Street, May Street, Gilbert Road, Murray Road, George Street, Jacka Street and Elizabeth Street, including McNamara Street, Murphy Street, Symons Street, Dunstan Street, Benambra Street, Grampian Street, Charles Street, Tynan Street, Sheffield Street and Bartlett Street.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the houses around Preston Primary junior campus -- with special thanks to Senator Jana Stewart and Ari Stewart for joining us… 

-- We spoke to a lot of people about the Victorian Labor Government's proposed $3.5 million upgrade to Preston Primary.
-- People were also strongly interested in what could be done to revitalise or improve the Plenty Road shops, with some asking what happened to the northbound component of tram stop #52.
-- The pandemic health measures continued to be a common point of discussion.
-- One resident raised a point about the bus stop near Preston Station on Murray Road: because it's so close to St Georges Road, the traffic often prevents the bus pulling up (or vice versa, the bus prevents the traffic moving into the left-hand lane). They suggested an inset bus stop as part of any upgrade to Preston Market.
-- We also discussed climate change, Preston Market generally, distrust of politicians, traditional owner land rights, traffic speed along Wood Street and Shakespeare Avenue, pensions, public housing and government spending.

One woman chatted to us remotely via her Google Nest doorbell (she was at a friend's place in West Preston), which was a bit strange but also kind of impressive!

Streets door-knocked: those enclosed by Wood Street, Plenty Road, Tyler Street and Tennyson Avenue, including Goldsmith Avenue, Shakespeare Avenue, Ellison Street, Bowden Street and Hawker Avenue.

Door-knocking feedback for the houses east of Seston Street...

-- We continued to get positive feedback about the new GP respiratory clinic, which helps people with asthma, hay fever, emphysema, COVID and other respiratory illnesses.
-- We also continued to get positive feedback on the $250 energy compare bonus. Last week, the Premier announced that if the Victorian Labor Government is re-elected, the bonus will be repeated in March.

-- We also discussed the pandemic response, rewilding Darebin Creek, disability support pensions, public housing, storm water drainage in Kirby Street, and the Victorian Labor Government's sick pay scheme for casual workers.

Door-knocking feedback for the houses around Reservoir East Primary -- with special thanks to my mum and brother who came out to help!

-- People were very positive about the new kindergarten being built at the primary school. The Andrew Labor Government is partnering with Darebin Council to build a three-room centre on the site with 66 places. Hopefully, having the centre next to the school will help with transition and drop-offs.
-- As per our previous post, the roundabout was a source of concern for a number of people, particularly with respect to pedestrian safety.
-- People also raised crime as an issue.
-- We had a good chat about the recent allied health EBA with the Victorian Government, and the way in which healthcare workers can't necessarily take protected action if it might affect patients' health.
-- We also chatted about sustainability, over-development, Preston Market, the different rights for public housing and community housing tenants, and the different pay arrangements for the workers who support those housing types. 

We were told that the fish and chip shop on Yarra Avenue was the best in Melbourne, and can confirm that it was very good!

Street door-knocked: those enclosed by Boldrewood Parade, North Road and Gisborne Crescent, including Genoa Avenue and the part of Yarra Avenue near the shops.

post_text: Groups like Friends of Edwardes Lake do an amazing job. Yesterday, another 3,600 plants were planted on the northern side of the lake thanks to Kate, Alex, Morris and the other volunteers. post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the households between Regent Station and the reservoirs…

-- There was strong support in the area for the Victorian Labor Government's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, and strong support for continuing the public health measures.
-- For residents on the Spring Street side of the tracks, the traffic can be a challenge: for example, trying to cross as a pedestrian near Moore Crescent or trying to turn out of Berwick Street in a vehicle.
-- Some people would like safety gates installed at the pedestrian crossing on the north of Regent Station. There are already gates at the southern end.
-- We had an interesting discussion about whether the service reservoirs would always be needed, and the potential to re-wild that land.
-- We also discussed health policy, Preston Market, parking issues, and the history of the housing on Crawley Street -- some of which date back to the nineteenth century!

One of the great things about door-knocking is getting to meet a really diverse range of people. One woman was 92 and had fled Belarus in World War II by stowing away with the retreating Germans! 

Streets door-knocked: the area enclosed by Powell Street, High Street, the service reservoirs and Spring Street, including Crawley Street, Sharpe Street, Down Street, Garden Street and the southern side of Berwick Street.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the houses around the Victorian Labor Government's new respiratory GP clinic at Your Community Health in Blake Street…

-- There was lots of positive feedback about the clinic. Between COVID-19 and flu season, a lot of people had used it already.
-- The streets to the west of the clinic have a higher proportion of retired residents. In those streets, we discussed pension rates, postal voting and the NDIS (the National Disability Insurance Scheme). We also discussed a number of public housing-related issues, including maintenance, parking and security.
-- As per our previous posts, we spoke to a number of healthcare workers who raised the impact of the pandemic on their workforce. Supporting healthcare workers has been a key priority for the Victorian Labor Government. In addition to the 22,000 healthcare worked that Labor has already recruited to the public system, we have committed to recruiting 24,000 more, including more paramedics and triple-zero staff. 
-- A number of people raised crime and community safety issues, including street lighting on Summerhill Avenue and Seston Street.
-- There was concern that new townhouse developments were unnecessarily removing mature trees.
-- We also discussed the Victorian Labor Government's new tenancy laws, schools, pre-prep, street parking, and the potholes from the recent rain.

A shout out to the crew at 100 Blake Street, who were especially welcoming!

Streets door-knocked: the area enclosed by Crevelli Street, Summerhill Road, Seston Street and Blake Street, including those parts of Nisbett Street, Clingin Street, Andrews Avenue (and its courts), and Kirby Steet, plus the extension of Blake Street towards Eisenhower.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the houses between Purinuan Road and Darebin Creek…

-- With respect to Clements Reserve, we got a similar response to our earlier door-knocking to the west of the reserve. People wanted the contamination addressed but also felt that issues related to the broader park area were important. 
-- A number of people mentioned traffic speeds, and the safety of the Boldrewood and Broadway roundabout.
-- As is often the case, we ran into people working on Victoria's 'Big Build' -- the suite of Labor transport projects that includes the 110 level-crossing removals, the rail link to Melbourne Airport, the new Metro rail tunnel, and North East Link. There are over 18,000 people working on those projects, and so far everyone we've met has wanted to see Labor re-elected so the projects continue.
-- We went past the sheep farm at the end of Rathcown Road! As far as we know, this is the only farm left in Reservoir. Apparently the owners have to pay 'vacant residential' penalty rates because there's no agricultural exemption for Darebin ratepayers any more!
-- We also discussed rewilding Darebin Creek, finding a new home for Keon Park Boxing Club, reviewing rock-climbing bans in the Grampians, protecting Preston Market, providing more parking on Rathcown Street, and changing the permit system for prescribing medicinal cannabis.

While we were in the area, we had the pleasure of meeting June Toohey, who had lived in Reservoir for 92 of her 95 years -- the longest-serving Reservoir resident we've met so far! She said there was definitely a lot more farmland when she moved in.

Streets door-knocked: Chennies Street, Rathcown Road east of the reserve, and the border formed by Purinuan Road and Nutwood Street.

post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the houses between Bell Street and Preston Market…

-- There was a lot of support for the level-crossing removal project, and people were excited about the new parks! Having said that, there were some people who had lived through a lot of disruption, and people as far away as Clifton Grove had been affected by the noise.
-- There was also strong support for the Victorian Labor Government's solar rebate program.
-- We door-knocked a couple of professional urban planners, which led to some detailed conversations about Preston Market. Some of the points and principles discussed included: 'Should all the carparks be maintained, and if so, should they be converted to a multi-storey or underground format, or left as they are?', 'Should the current trading hours, with no trading on Mondays or Tuesdays, be enforced as a permanent aspect of the precinct?', and 'Would more office space benefit the precinct (for instance, moving a government authority there) or would it negatively impact the sense of community?'.
-- We had a couple of conversations about the High Street shops between Bruce and Bell, and whether or not that section could be uplifted.
-- We also discussed bike lanes, apartment development, Maroondah Hospital, the David Street chinaberry trees and the difficulties of convincing landlords to make energy efficiency improvements (despite the financial incentives offered by the Victorian Labor Government).

Streets door-knocked: Herbert Street, Emery Street, Donovan Street, Bruce Street (east of the train line), Mary Street, Clifton Grove, the southern side of David Street, and the adjacent parts of High Street and Bell Street (though they were mostly apartments).

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for Elizabeth Street (north of Murray), Murray Road, Malcolm Street, McGowan Avenue and its courts…

-- This is a fascinating part of the world for the high number of brick duplexes. I was told by a McGowan Ave resident that they were built by an Austrian migrant who wanted to encourage a communal atmosphere. It seems to have worked!
-- We've discussed the safety of Elizabeth Street in previous posts. Some residents in the section just north of Murray also wanted a speed reduction to 50 kilometres per hour. 
-- We chatted to a number of people about the linear reserve. There is a strong sense that the space is not as well used as it could be. There is the beginning of a footpath at Elizabeth Street but otherwise it is mostly just grass. There are some well-established gums near North Street and it's not clear why there couldn't be more native vegetation, or a footpath, or both.
-- We had a good discussion about the accessibility of local public transport. There are three tram lines in the area but the nearest level-access stop is the North Coburg terminus. This is something the Victorian Labor Government has worked hard to improve. Of the 1,700 tram stops in Melbourne, about a quarter are now fully accessible. The 527 to the new Preston Station is an alternative option for accessible travel to the city. 
-- As per our previous bus route post, service frequency on the 526 was an issue. It doesn't run on Sundays.
-- We also discussed Preston Market, street lights in Malcolm Street, level crossing removals, petrol prices, the Dunstan Street dog off-leash area ('Does it need lighting and fencing?'), community batteries, and the installation of solar in aged care and social housing.

On a sad note, we knocked on the door of Lily Coy, a local Labor legend who was always full of energy and great ideas. Unfortunately, Lily was in hospital and passed away a couple of days later. Her passion will be sorely missed by her comrades. Vale Lily Jean Coy, 13.01.1933 – 18.09.2022.

post_text:
Following our door-knocking around Elizabeth Street and Murray Road, we met with local residents to discuss pedestrian and cyclist safety on Elizabeth Street specifically. Brent Houghton and Cate Hall from Coburg High joined us to discuss safe, active travel for their students.

The following points were made.

-- A high volume of pedestrians regularly cross Elizabeth Street either north or south of the Murray Road intersection. Over a hundred students cross it each day, mainly to access Coburg High. The Newlands shops and Merri Creek parks draw pedestrians from the east. And people often cross it to catch the 527 or 526 bus.
-- Cyclists also cross the section at a number of points. Elizabeth Street is the border between Darebin and Merri-bek councils, and both councils have committed to a strategic cycling corridor that will cross somewhere near Hope Street.
-- However, the section lacks options for crossing safely. The current speed limit is 60 kilometres per hour and the two crests (at Murray Road and the cemetery) reduce visibility. There are no traffic islands or mid-block crossing points south of Murray Road. For people with prams, wheel-chairs or scooters, there are few ramps.

We have passed on these comments to Ben Carroll, the Minister for Roads and Road Safety. We also passed on some specific comments about the intersections at Murray Road and Bell Street. Thanks to Sarah (pictured) who has taken a lead role in advocating for Elizabeth Street safety improvements.

Thanks to our volunteers who helped door-knock the houses near the Visy plant over a couple of very wet days! We mainly spoke to residents about the Visy issue. However, people took the opportunity to raise other issues, so we have summarised them here.

-- Trucks were a frequent source of concern close to the industrial areas. Notably, speed bumps and roundabouts can be noisy when trucks go over them and their loads bounce. The speed bumps near the Radford and Broadhurst intersection were a specific example.
-- People also raised other industry-related issues: light pollution, noise pollution, competition for parking spots, debris on the roads, and dust.
-- We talked about the need for a safe crossing point on Banbury Road, where people cross to the park.
-- We discussed service frequency on the 553 bus and the 11 tram.
-- A few people raised access to parks and playgrounds (though most of the houses were close to either Edwardes Lake or Merri Creek).
-- There was support for the Victorian Labor Government's upgrades of local high schools, including Preston High and William Ruthven Secondary College.
-- We also discussed immigration, irresponsible drivers, child abuse, health, cost of living, on-street parking, Preston Market, animal protection, townhouse development, the need for more bike paths, and the possibility of a bridge over Merri Creek at the end of Edwardes Street.

A lot of people had lived in the area for a long time, especially at the northern end around Broadhurst. We chatted to Nino who had been there 53 years. When he moved in, the area was mostly paddocks and he had to protect his garden from cattle!

The Victorian Labor Government is currently reviewing bus routes across the northern suburbs. Below is the bus-related feedback we've received so far from door-knocking. If you have any other comments on bus routes, let us know. The review closes on 16 October!

-- A number of people have raised service frequency, particularly on the 527, 552, 553, 561 and 567 routes.
-- If you're on the 'extension loops' for either the 553 or 558, which go around Edwardes Lake and the Central Creek reserve respectively, services can be very infrequent.
-- There is a lot of support for the Victorian Labor Government's new electric buses.
-- The 558 through north-east Reservoir can be pretty confusing with its clockwise and anti-clockwise variations. It also stops just after midday on Saturday, because that's when the shops used to close (for those of us old enough to remember the 1980s!). 
-- Residents in Station Street and Henry Street were concerned about the speed of the 567 through their streets.
-- La Trobe staff and students were pleased that the 301 express shuttle, which was introduced by the Labor government, has been made permanent.
-- Generally speaking, people think it would be good if bus timetables and train timetables were more closely aligned.
-- There was support for more universal bus accessibility.

If you would like to contribute directly to the review, you can do so here:

   https://engage.vic.gov.au/project/busreform/page/melbournes-northern-suburbs

post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for the households around Regent station (both the Spring Street and High Street sides)…

-- There was a strong feeling that public transport options for students needed to be safe and secure.
-- Having said that, there were mixed views on the Regent station car park lighting: whether it was too bright or not.
-- There were also mixed views on the Preston market redevelopment, but most people favoured an outcome that was much closer to council's latest proposal than the owners'.
-- Following the Victorian Labor Government's upgrades to Preston station, Reservoir station and Keon Park station, people naturally wondered about the possibility of removing the level crossing at Regent Street and upgrading Regent station as well -- although one resident noted that the water pipes might make it difficult. The Labor Government has announced that if it is re-elected, the Frankston, Lilydale and Pakenham lines will cleared of all boom-gates by 2029, allowing even more frequent train services on those lines. 
-- People on Station and Henry streets were concerned about the speed of the 567 buses through their streets.
-- There was strong support for the Victorian Labor Government's solar battery rebate.
-- On the western side of the station, some people wanted the right-hand turn from Regent Street into Spring Street to change back to its old configuration.
-- A smaller resident raised the topic of playgrounds! She would like more shaded play areas!
-- Other topics included immigration, police integrity, how health waiting lists should be triaged, and whether the AFL was a vehicle for American cultural imperialism.

It was great to have some new volunteers join us to door-knock the streets around the contaminated Clements Reserve.

-- People were obviously worried about the contamination and wanted it cleaned up. Parents were taking their children to TW Andrews Reserve instead, which is fortunately only 700 metres up the road (admittedly a long way sometimes with a toddler!).
-- A lot of people took the opportunity to raise other issues with the Darebin Creek parklands, including litter, the shortage of bins for rubbish and dog waste, the lack of lighting, weed infestation, and whether the area was too dog-friendly (or not dog-friendly enough!).
-- People were very positive about the Victorian Labor Government's upgrade of Reservoir Station, albeit with one suggestion that Broadway and Edwardes be joined by lifting the station even higher!
-- We talked about bike paths and the quality of bike lanes. We also talked about roads, including the Boldrewood/Broadway roundabout and the right-hand turning lane out of Boldrewood into Plenty Road.
-- We chatted about public housing issues, including the way that rents can change significantly if the reference market rate is revised at the same time that a household member starts working.
-- Other topics included Preston Market, HECS fees, and the impact of the Victorian Labor Government's rental reforms.

post_text:
Door-knocking feedback on the new Keon Park station…

-- We door-knocked about 300 houses and businesses on both sides of the tracks. In general, people were very positive. The most common response was "We're looking forward to it" or words to that effect.
-- On the Hughes Parade side, there was a lot of support for the new traffic lights, which will make pedestrian access safer.
-- On the Johnson Street side, a number of people asked about parking: "Will there be enough for the project workers?", "Will there be enough for travellers once the station is complete?", "Will there be spill-over into the side streets?", and "Will there be two-way access to the station carpark from Johnson Street?".
-- Several residents pointed out that a significant source of pressure on the Keon Parade intersection was the fact that it was one of only two places in Reservoir where drivers could cross the railway line (something discussed in previous posts). People asked whether the sky-rail could be extended south to allow for a third crossing at Hughes Parade, Hickford Street or even Ruthven Station. 
-- Relatedly, some people worried that if the proposed carpark had access to both Johnson Street and High Street, it would become an informal shortcut to avoid Keon Parade, and people would drive through more quickly and frequently than is safe.
-- People were also concerned about the High Street entrance to the carpark.  
-- There was strong support for the planting of native trees, shrubs and groundcover.
-- There was also strong support for the bright colour scheme and bold architectural elements. People were positive about the new Preston Station and said they wanted something similar.

We have passed on the feedback to the minister, Jacinta Allan. We are also following up a couple of other matters related to the apartments nearest to the sky-rail and the vacant private land on the eastern edge of the site.

Door-knocking feedback for Keon Park… We mainly spoke to residents and businesses about the new train station. However, people took the opportunity to raise other issues, so we've summarised them here. 

-- On the Hughes Parade side of the tracks, people raised bus access for students, the bumps caused by the ironbarks on Botha Avenue, school options, and access to the other side of the railway. It really is a striking feature of Reservoir that it has such a long section of railway -- over two kilometres -- with no road crossings and very few pedestrian crossings. As some people say, the railway really is the 'Berlin Wall'. It is hard to think of anywhere else in Melbourne where a suburban area is so divided.
-- On the Johnson Street side of the tracks, people were generally positive about the new apartment blocks, which they hoped would uplift the shopping strip. The Victorian Labor Government's energy compare bonus continued to be popular. 
-- Other topics of discussion included the handling of the pandemic, Maroondah Hospital, gas exploration and the efficiency of public housing spending.

We grabbed a burger afterwards from Bambams -- can recommend the standard burger or the 'Colonel Mustard' vegan option (might be worth a review, The Prestonian!).

The streets door-knocked were Asquith Street, Eyre Street, Hughes Parade (east of Eyre), High Street (north of Asquith), Leichardt Crescent, Mahoneys Road and Merrilands Road (both east of Asquith), Arundel Avenue and Keon Parade and Liston Avenue and Lloyd Avenue (all west of Finton Grove), Falk Avenue and Johnson Street.

post_text:
Door-knocking feedback for Regent Street (near High Street), William Street, West Street, Olver Street, Cambrian Avenue and Spencer Street…

-- William Street was the most engaged street any of us have ever door-knocked. In almost two hours, we only got halfway up the street -- lots of detailed conversations!
-- The people who back on to the railway have obviously had to put up with significant disruption during the removal of the level crossing, and they deserve our gratitude for their forbearance. There are still a few outstanding issues, but overall, most people's interest was what would happen next, particularly with the railway reserve. I understand that there will be some more native trees (a good start!) but we're finding out.
-- At the Regent Street end, where there was less disruption, people were keen for a level-crossing removal of their own!
-- We talked to people about safety for pedestrians crossing High Street, and safety for pedestrians in the Woolworths carpark.
-- Had a couple of interesting discussions about gardens, and specifically whether the classic 'lawn with flower beds' arrangement is a poor choice for urban heat management and biodiversity.
-- Almost every time we chat to someone who works in health, we hear about the impacts of the pandemic on the workforce. It's been mentioned in the comments here too. Supporting the health workforce is a huge priority for the Victorian Labor Government. Since Labor was elected, we have added over 22,000 healthcare workers to the public health service (an increase of 30%), and the Health Minister, Mary-Anne Thomas MP, recently announced that she would recruit or train another 7,000. The Victorian Labor Government has introduced new retention payments. It has provided more funding for undergraduate positions. It has made studying nursing or midwifery free. There has been a real effort to leave no stone unturned, but of course if people have other ideas we would love to hear them.
-- Other topics of discussion included bulk billing, the 'El Jannah traffic jam', Preston High, Preston Market and Preston Station.

If we missed you, feel free to get in touch. We'll post any updates in the comments below.

post_title: Nathan Lambert MP added a new photo.
post_text:
Hi, I'm Nathan Lambert, the Labor candidate for the electorate of Preston.

The electorate lies between Darebin Creek and Merri Creek on the lands of the Wurundjeri people.

It is a diverse area, and one in which the Victorian Government is involved in people's lives in a lot of different ways. 

The government runs local schools and health services. It makes decisions about planning and public transport. Under the leadership of Daniel Andrews, it has introduced major new programs for social housing, family violence and mental health.

All of these services require community input if they're to be the best they can be. That in turn requires good representatives: people who can seek out those affected by government decisions and listen to their ideas, concerns and lived experiences.  

Like everyone involved in politics, I have my own passions — fairness, inclusion and sustainability. But I also strongly believe that the role of an elected representative is about the collective, not the individual.

Preston and Reservoir have long working-class histories. Some of the factories have gone, but the ethos remains. As someone said to me, "People are more communal here. They're not competitive. They don't judge you by the clothes you wear or the car you drive" (or if you don't drive at all!).

If elected, I’ll work hard to represent Preston and Reservoir in a way that reflects Preston and Reservoir. I'll be enthusiastic about projects that benefit all of us and warier about those that benefit a select few. I'll support our artists, our students and our natural environment. Above all, I'll try to make sure that our decisions are made collectively, in a way that doesn't leave anyone out or leave anyone behind.
